The name Anāthapiṇḍada (rendered from Tibetan མགོན་མེད་ཟས་སྦྱིན, meaning "feeder of the unprotected") is the standard epithet of the great lay patron Sudatta; both names are traditional and interchangeable in the literature. The rendering follows the most natural doctrinal reading: the exemplary precedent set by the Blessed One in his bodhisattva lives is cited as the normative basis for Ānanda's obedience to the Blessed One's command.  The names "Vāsuladattā," "Āvanti," "Giribhadra," and "Sagā" represent renderings of Tibetan phonetic transcriptions of what would be Sanskrit originals: བཙུན་མོ་ཕྲེང་ལྡན་མ (likely Mālikā or Vāsuladattā), རྒྱལ་རིགས་དབྱར་ཚུལ་མ (a royal lady whose name is uncertain), and རི་དགས་འཛིན་གྱི་མ་ས་ག (possibly a matronymic). The final instruction — that the stūpa of the one who has passed into nirvāṇa should be placed where Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana used to sit relative to the Tathāgata — reflects a rule about positioning reliquary stūpas for disciples to the sides or in front of the Tathāgata's shrine, echoing Vinaya architectural norms. The passage is the Tibetan canonical version of the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, the discourse on the turning of the wheel of Dharma, presenting the twelve-aspect formulation of the Four Noble Truths: three rounds (knowing what each truth is, knowing what task pertains to each, and knowing that task has been accomplished) across four truths, yielding twelve aspects. The term rendered "vision arose" translates the formulaic mig skyes so, corresponding to Sanskrit cakṣur udapādi, literally "an eye arose," a technical expression for the arising of insight-vision; "vision arose" captures this without importing the odd literalism of "an eye was born" while remaining faithful to the idiom.

"Nārada" renders Drang-srong Mi-dkar-ba (literally "the white-bodied sage"), while Nālada is used directly from the syllables Na-la-da in the Tibetan.  The phrase rendered "the nectar of immortality" translates the Tibetan term for amṛta, the deathless — here signifying the attainment of awakening or nirvāṇa.

The figure Nārada here is presented with complexity: initially portrayed as a venerable sage, the closing lines describe him as one corrupted by wrong views and given to deception. This is consistent with certain Indo-Tibetan narrative traditions in which the Brahmanical sage Nārada appears in a critical or ambivalent role within Buddhist literature. The phrase "white-clad sage" renders a Tibetan term that may indicate a particular sect or status; the epithet is kept as given.

The verse "by those who discern only the lesser marks" conveys that those of limited discernment, seeing the bodhisattva's bodily marks, predict worldly kingship over the four continents, whereas one of clear insight like Nārada perceives the marks of full buddhahood.  The four-line verse is a well-known set of impermanence aphorisms found across Pāli and Sanskrit Buddhist literature. The rendering follows the natural rhetorical parallelism of the original.

The name Nāḷada (distinct from Nārada) is established in the narrative as a new character derived from Nārada by bone-kinship; the Tibetan etymology plays on "rus" (bone) connecting the two names, which is difficult to render in English without awkwardness and so is left implicit.

The phrase rendered "the settled domain of the great earth" reflects a technical administrative or cosmological expression in the Tibetan that is somewhat opaque; the translation gives its most plausible sense in context.  The names Sā Tsho Ma, Ri Dags Skyes, and Grags Dzin Ma appear to be Tibetan renderings of Sanskrit names for the women in the prince's retinue before his renunciation. The context parallels standard accounts of the Buddha's life, but the specific Sanskrit equivalents are not recoverable with certainty from this passage alone.

The phrase rendered as "the five fields of knowledge" refers to the classical Indian pañcavidyā, the five sciences traditionally mastered by an educated prince.

The term rendered "pressed into essence" for ཉིང་ཁུར་བྱས་པ refers to churned or concentrated milk-porridge; the exact preparation is a detail of the standard biography of the Buddha's acceptance of food from Sujātā, here adapted with different names for the women.

The translation preserves this as-is, since it is a feature of the original text, not an error in rendering.  The verse at the end presents a list of inauspicious omens in a riddle-like format. The term "ས་འཛིན་པ" (lord of the earth) is used both as the guard's title and as an address to the king; context disambiguates each use. The section heading "The Vinaya of minor matters, the twenty-fourth section" (འདུལ་བ་ཕྲན་ཚེགས་ཀྱི་གཞི། བམ་པོ་ཉི་ཤུ་བཞི་པ།) appears mid-passage, marking a scribal or editorial division in the canonical text. The phrase rendered "twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection" translates a standard Abhidharma formulation: the view of a transitory collection (Sanskrit satkāyadṛṣṭi) comprises twenty sub-views regarding the five aggregates (each viewed fourfold as self, as belonging to self, as in self, or as self in it), and these are destroyed upon stream-entry.

The verse on karma not being lost is a well-known canonical gāthā found in several sūtra and Vinaya contexts, sometimes attributed to the ālayavijñāna doctrine in later scholastic literature, though here it functions as a straightforward statement on karmic inevitability without necessarily implying Yogācāra metaphysics.

The monk's outburst — "This thing has neither life nor breath; what offense did the Blessed One Kāśyapa see in it that he made it a basis for training?" — is a reference to Vinaya rules protecting plants and trees, which the monk is mocking at the moment of his disrobing. The line "sངས་རྒྱས་དགོངས་པས་ཆ་ལུགས་བསྒྱུར་ནས་ནི" means literally "having transformed his deportment or bearing by the Buddha's intention" — rendered as "through the Buddha's intention his bearing was changed," which captures the miraculous instantaneous transformation of the newly ordained monk's appearance by the Tathāgata's power.

The final section parallels the famous Kātyāyana Sūtra (Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.15 / Saṃyuktāgama), one of the most important canonical expositions of the Middle Way between eternalism and nihilism. The teaching here closely follows that sūtra's doctrine that right view avoids the two extremes of "exists" and "does not exist" by attending instead to the arising and cessation of suffering through dependent origination. The line rendered "Vaiśravaṇa's steward drove him on" refers to Pradyota being driven like a draft animal; "the steward of Vaiśravaṇa" is an epithet playing on the name Dhanavardhana, who is elsewhere identified with the yakṣa treasurer figure. The line "Earth and forest soared into the sky" is a riddle-kenning for the palanquin carrying Pradyota. These are intentional riddles sung by the bystanders, and the opacity is original to the text.

The phrase rendered "the god Dhanavardhana has given this" reflects a deliberate fiction Śarva orders to be maintained: that Pradyota's arrival was a divine gift rather than a kidnapping, to protect the political secret.  The passage describes Dhanavardhana's elaborate plot to fulfill — or appear to fulfill — the queen's vow while engineering the death of King Śarva's son. The queen's vow involves a seven-day fast and a ritual wrapping in flower garlands followed by being seated at the enclosure gate; Dhanavardhana exploits this vow as the mechanism for throwing the prince from the enclosure wall. The identity of "the god" in the queen's speech refers to the captive king, using the honorific "lha" as a form of royal address, not to a divine being. This dual usage of "lha" — both as the deity Dhanavardhana's name-element and as a royal honorific in the queen's speech — is a notable feature of the passage; the translation renders each instance according to context.  The closing epithet applied to the new king renders three Tibetan terms together: "fierce" (gtum po), "supremely radiant" (rab snang), and "without rival" (gran zla med pa). These appear to be epithets embedded in or functioning as a proper name or a descriptive title for the successor king; the text does not give a separate personal name here, so they are rendered as descriptive epithets.  The name rendered "Rabhasa Prabhā" corresponds to the Tibetan "གཏུམ་པོ་རབ་སྣང་" (fierce, supremely radiant), which is the king introduced at the end of the preceding passage. This is the same king described there as fierce and radiant as the sun.

The name "Lotus-Hearted" renders "པད་མའི་སྙིང་པོ་ཅན་" (one who has a lotus heart/core), which appears to be a personal name or epithet of the king's antagonist.

"Āryā" renders "'འཕགས་རྒྱལ་," a term for the noble realm or country; this may be a place name requiring identification from the broader textual context.

"Dambha" renders "'འདམ་བུ་," treated here as a proper name for the elephant.

The final sentence is cut off mid-passage in the source text; the translation ends accordingly.  The phrase rendered "the land of setting-down-stones" translates the toponym that has been consistently used in the preceding context for Balaṅkya's destination; it is a proper place-name in this narrative, not a descriptive phrase, but the Tibetan is rendered literally as no Sanskrit or standard equivalent is established in the passage.

The minister's remarks to the potter and the dung beetle are deliberately ambiguous, each capable of being heard as a general moral maxim or as a pointed personal jibe at the king — which is precisely the dramatic irony the text exploits. The translation preserves this ambiguity.  The term rendered as "god" throughout this passage is an honorific form of address from the minister to the king, a standard idiom of Indian courtly speech in which a king is addressed as "divine majesty" or simply "god." It is not a reference to a deity.

The phrase rendered "unfired pottery vessels" (སྣོད་སོ་མ) refers to raw, sun-dried but not yet kiln-fired pots, which are fragile; this detail is essential to the meaning of the minister's first explanation.  The passage presents several interpretive challenges. The term translated throughout as "spy-women" or "eavesdroppers" (Tibetan: phra men ma) refers to female spies or informants — possibly also understood as demonesses or she-demons (srin mo) in the proclamation at the close, which conflates the two groups deliberately in the ruse. The final line's proclamation invokes "the pledge of the mother of the gods" (lha ni ma'i dam tshig) as the authoritative summons, a ritual fiction designed to gather the targets together. The text breaks off mid-sentence at "And they thought," indicating the passage continues beyond the excerpt provided.  The phrase rendered "those who lived by the chopper's trade" translates a term literally meaning "those who live by the chopper or cleaver," that is, butchers or slaughtermen, here serving as executioners — the point being that the king employed men already habituated to killing for this mass beheading.

The six opening syllables of the dream-verses are given as a mnemonic device in the text: each monosyllabic word is the first syllable of the corresponding verse. The verses appear to be laments spoken by the slain brahmins — now recognizing in the dream-speech of the dead that they have been cast into hell as a consequence of their previous evil deeds as she-demons. This doctrinal interpretation should be understood in the context of the narrative.  The six verses keyed to the six sky-sounds form an embedded literary structure; each verse is introduced by its opening syllable or word, which serves as a mnemonic heading. The translation preserves this structure while making it natural for listening.

The phrase rendered "five finest limbs nourished there" translates a term literally meaning "the five best limbs fattened/nourished," which in the context of blood-sacrifice likely refers to five prime sacrificial victims selected and prepared. The exact referent is somewhat compressed in the Tibetan.

The passage ends mid-sentence in the source, which is reflected in the translation.  The six earth-sounds and six sky-sounds function as acrostics: each word names the opening syllable of the verse that follows. This is a recognized literary device in Indian narrative and the Tibetan text signals it explicitly. The rendering preserves the acrostic frame by heading each verse with its key word.

The name Kātyāyanī's son refers to Mahākātyāyana, one of the principal disciples of the Buddha, renowned for his skill in doctrinal exposition. The cow's counsel to seek him out is a pivot in the narrative.  The term rendered "otters" translates a Tibetan word that can refer to otters or similar water-dwelling creatures; the precise species is contextually uncertain but "otter" is the standard identification in Vinaya commentarial literature.  The mountain name "Tumldän" renders the Tibetan Ri bo Gtum ldan. The literal meaning is something like "the mountain possessing fierceness," but as it functions as a proper place name in context it is left in transliterated form rather than translated. If a conventional Sanskrit or standard English rendering exists in the source text's tradition it has not been preserved here.

The phrase rendered "procures even a single eye's worth" is genuinely difficult. The Tibetan reads mig ya gcig kyang 'jor byed pa, literally "one who acquires even a single eye." In context the crow appears to be saying that even someone who takes so little as a single egg or morsel — or, alternatively, one who profits by a single eye's amount through dishonest means — has caused her loss. The intended sense within the verse is that the horse-keeper's destructive act, however small it might seem, ultimately freed her (and her young) from some form of suffering, perhaps meaning that death ended their distress. The doctrinal or narrative logic here is somewhat opaque and may reflect a variant reading.  The place-names Yavana, Siṃhala, Vaṅgāla, and Kaliṅga are left in approximate Sanskrit equivalents as they appear in the text and denote, respectively, the Greek or western lands, Sri Lanka, Bengal, and the Kaliṅga region of eastern India. The Tibetan for Vaṅgāla is rendered as such rather than "Bengal" to preserve the proper-name register of the passage.

The phrase rendered "a different person in the funeral litter" follows the context established in the preceding passage about the litter-bearer; the Tibetan gdung ma yang gzhan zhig bcug literally means "he also put another person in the gdung ma," where gdung ma refers to the funeral or carrying litter referenced earlier.

The phrase skya bseng gi bu mo is rendered "daughter of the śramaṇa woman" literally; it could also mean "daughter of a poor woman" or "daughter of a mendicant woman." The context does not fully resolve this.  The passage distinguishes between the Blessed One's "worldly thought" and his "supramundane thought" — a doctrinal point about the range of the buddha's cognition: his ordinary operational awareness is perceptible even to insects, whereas his transcendent awareness is beyond the reach of even śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. This is a standard teaching on the incomprehensibility of a buddha's highest gnosis.

The term rendered "Śivā" for Gopālā's mother comes from the preceding context where "Gopālā's mother, Śivā" appears; here the Tibetan has only "Gopālā's mother, Śivā," consistent with the preceding passage rendering.

The term མ་ཧེ (mahe) is a loanword for the water buffalo (Skt. mahiṣa), rendered accordingly.  The epithet rendered "Bimbisāra, the artisan-king of Rājagṛha" translates a Tibetan phrase meaning literally "the artisan-skilled, form-possessing essence of Rājagṛha," which appears to be a circumlocution identifying Bimbisāra as a patron of fine craftsmanship. The Tibetan name བཟོ་སྦྱངས་གཟུགས་ཅན་སྙིང་པོ is unusual and may be a descriptive epithet rather than the king's proper name; the identification with Bimbisāra rests on context (king of Rājagṛha, first to offer cooked food to the Saṅgha), which is a well-attested distinction of Bimbisāra in the tradition.

The name Supriya (བཟང་ལྡན) for the householder of Vārāṇasī follows the probable Sanskrit reconstruction; the Tibetan literally means "possessing excellence/goodness."  The creature called "thī-ba" is a small bird (likely a wren or similar passerine) whose Tibetan name lacks a clean English equivalent. Rather than invent a misleading common name, I have retained "thī-ba" throughout as a proper name for the creature, treating it as the story treats it — as a named narrative character. Listeners familiar with Jātaka literature will recognize the type.

The attendant's speech beginning "Indeed, Your Majesty, I sought her out and killed her" is a continuation of his ruse from the preceding passage: he has not actually killed Śāntā but hidden her, and he now speaks deceptively to the king before telling the parable to cool the king's fury. This dramatic irony is clear in context.  The verse on the "two kinds of blind" hinges on a contrast between those who are physically blind from birth and those who are morally blind through rejecting the Dharma or the law — a standard didactic trope in Buddhist narrative literature. The second set adds those who hold sinful views and those who disregard civil or moral law.

The phrase rendered "plays the go-between" for ཕོ་ཉའི་ཕོ་ཉ is literally "a messenger of a messenger," meaning one who acts as an intermediary courier, here condemned in the context of carrying illicit communications. The specific nuance of ཕོ་ཉའི་ཕོ་ཉ alongside མངག་གཞུག་པ་ཡི་མངག་གཞུག and འཕྱོན་མ is that all three involve deceptive or exploitative use of a role of trust; the rendering attempts to capture this social sense.  The final two lines are the opening of a summary verse that breaks off mid-passage; they are translated as they stand without completion.

The verse about the net plays on a sustained pun in the Tibetan: the word rendered as "net" also carries the sense of "by means of" or "through connections," creating a deliberate double meaning that the original exploits in each line. The translation attempts to preserve this where possible.

The line about the wrestler's son is rendered as "for one who is to slay, there is always the means to do it without fail," reflecting the sense that a trained killer naturally finds a way; the exact force of the final line is slightly compressed in the Tibetan and this reading is the most defensible.  The verse on the four kinds of deceivers presents some syntactic ambiguity. The fourth item, "dividing what belongs to the powerful," could alternatively be rendered as "scattering among the powerful" or "dispersing to those of strength," depending on whether the object is what is distributed or to whom it goes. The rendering chosen fits the proverbial pattern of futile or absurd actions best.

The summary verse near the middle of the passage appears to be a mnemonic colophon enumerating the topics of the entire dialogue sequence, and its terms are intentionally compressed. "Grief and its attendants" renders a compound that literally means "craving, unconsidered action, grief-class," which fits the list of topics covered by the king's accusations.  The summary verse near the end is metrically and syntactically compressed; its four paired objects read as a list of things that are paradoxically trustworthy or worth attending to despite their problematic qualities. The precise pairing of each quality with its subject is ambiguous in the Tibetan, and the verse appears to function as a transitional summary of the preceding exchanges rather than a self-contained logical unit. The rendering given here follows the most natural reading of the grammatical structure.  The summary verse beginning "Sleeplessness, unwished-for things" appears to function as a colophon-like mnemonic enumerating the topics of the section just completed and those to follow; its terse compression makes the precise sequence of referents somewhat ambiguous, but the rendering reflects the most natural reading. The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the attendant's explanation of the nine torments, corresponding to the Tibetan text ending mid-construction.  The passage's threefold repetition of the nine-things formula appears to present three distinct psychological cases that are structurally parallel but doctrinally distinct. The second and third iterations appear to reverse the relational valence between the two parties involved, which produces some interpretive difficulty in the Tibetan. The rendering follows the most natural reading of the syntax as it stands.

The list of "ten without compassion" is a standard folk-ethical enumeration found in Vinaya-adjacent narrative literature; the rendering of each occupation follows established parallels in similar canonical lists.

The phrase rendered "fallow ground" for སླད་ས is somewhat uncertain; it may refer specifically to land that has been cultivated but left barren, and the explanation of why it "turns things away" is contained in the portion of text yet to be translated.  The phrase rendered "tamer of persons to be tamed, a charioteer, unsurpassed" reflects a standard epithet cluster for a buddha: one who tames those to be tamed and is the supreme charioteer or guide. The Tibetan here runs several epithets together without fully separating them, but they correspond to standard Sanskrit formulae found throughout the Vinaya and sūtra literature.

The expression "station of the finest bull of the herd" translates a standard epithet of the Buddha as foremost among beings, corresponding to Sanskrit vṛṣabhasthāna or similar.  The Tibetan term rendered as "the path that leads everywhere" is "kun du 'gro ba'i lam," which in the parallel Sanskrit lists of the ten powers corresponds to "sarvatragāminīṃ pratipadaṃ," the path leading to all destinations or the path to all rebirths. The rendering "the path that leads everywhere" preserves both the literal meaning and the technical doctrinal sense of knowing which karma leads to which realm of rebirth.

The passage ends mid-sentence as the Tibetan source text itself is cut off at that point.  The phrase rendered "having taken up actions and dharmas rooted in wrong view" (and its positive parallel) reflects a formulaic Pali-Tibetan locution meaning that these persons have adopted a course of conduct fully consonant with wrong or right view respectively. The term "dharmas" here means doctrines or principles (the things one upholds), not phenomena in a philosophical sense.

The name "Gośa" (Tibetan: གསོས་པ, literally "one who nourishes" or possibly a proper name transcription) appears here as the character who leads the cow-herder's mother to the king; the Tibetan is ambiguous as to whether this is a proper name or a descriptive epithet. The reading as a proper name is adopted here as contextually more natural, but a note on this is warranted.  The name Kanyākubja rendered from the Tibetan transliteration "ka nyā kub dza" — this is the city in northern India also known as Kanauj, and its appearance here as a gift from the king is consistent with the narrative's royal setting. The summary verse is a mnemonic colophon listing characters from the preceding story cycle; its terseness is intentional and the rendering is accordingly spare. The phrase rendered "the way of the Dharma of permanence" reflects the Tibetan "rtag chos kyi tshul," where "rtag" may mean "eternal" or "constant" in the sense of the Dharma's abiding character — the point is that the Dharma's way endures and is to be followed continually.  The phrase rendered "as a way of testing them" translates brtag pa'i bsam pas, literally "with a mind of examination or testing." The contrast between this wording in the Blessed One's speech and the slightly different phrasing bgam pa'i bsam pas, "with a mind of deceiving or entrapping them," in Ānanda's retelling to the monks is noteworthy and may reflect a deliberate distinction in the Tibetan: the Blessed One frames it neutrally as a test, while Ānanda characterizes the householder's intent as more adversarial. Both renderings follow the text as given.  The passage moves between two distinct narrative episodes without a marked break: the Vaiśālī episode concludes with the Vinaya ruling on precious vessels, and a new episode then opens in Śrāvastī. This abrupt transition is in the original and is not a translation error.

The phrase rendered "knowing moderation" translates a term meaning awareness of measure or restraint in eating and receiving, a standard Vinaya virtue; the context confirms this reading.  The name Prabhāvatī is a Sanskrit reconstruction of the Tibetan འོད་བཟང་མ (od bzang ma), meaning "she who is radiant with fine light." The text's own folk etymology connects it to the blazing of the house at birth. The rendering "Radiant with Light" reflects the Tibetan form; the Sanskrit Prabhāvatī is the standard equivalent found in parallel Sanskrit recensions.

The phrase "sages who had renounced attachment by the ordinary worldly path" renders the Tibetan འཇིག་རྟེན་པའི་ལམ་གྱིས་འདོད་ཆགས་དང་བྲལ་བའི་དྲང་སྲོང, referring to non-Buddhist ascetics or worldly meditators who have suppressed but not eradicated desire through mundane meditative paths — a standard doctrinal distinction.  The epithet "Wife-killer" renders the Tibetan "chung ma gsod pa," literally "killer of wives," which functions as a stigmatizing nickname in the narrative. The rendering "fined and penalized" for "dpya bar 'gyur ba'i las" reflects a probable legal or social penalty associated with the repeated deaths of his wives; the precise nature of this penalty is not specified in the text.  The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end, mid-enumeration of the body parts Śrī-prabhā is mentally cataloguing. This is a continuation passage and the list is clearly unfinished at the manuscript break point; the translation renders exactly what is present.

The phrase rendered "the keys and the crooked keys" reflects a distinction in the Tibetan between two types of keys; the precise technical difference is unclear from the text alone, but both terms appear to denote household keys of different kinds, symbolizing Śrī-prabhā's installation as household mistress.  The phrase "the fire of attachment at the tenth ground" is doctrinally striking: it says the fire of desire characteristic of beings at the tenth bodhisattva ground arose in her, which is an unusual formulation. In context it likely means an intensity of desire surpassing even the highest level — a hyperbolic expression indicating overwhelming passion rather than a technical claim that she was a tenth-ground bodhisattva. This is worth flagging as a doctrinal curiosity.

The closing phrase rendered as "what abided near her like a weapon's thrust" translates a term literally meaning "that which was present like a dagger" or "ready at hand like a weapon." The exact idiomatic force of this final clause is somewhat compressed in the Tibetan and likely signals that her karmic fruits were ripe and unavoidable — the image of a weapon poised to strike conveying inevitability.  The verse "Even across hundreds of aeons..." is a well-known canonical gāthā that appears in several Vinaya and Āgama sources; it is here rendered as verse consistent with its formulaic status.

The epithet translated as "Grove of Sages Who Speak Truth" renders a Tibetan gloss of the standard Isipatana (Pāli) or Ṛṣivadana (Sanskrit), the deer park at Vārāṇasī. The Tibetan phrase here is a semantic rendering rather than the usual transliteration.

The phrase rendered "maternal uncles" (Tibetan zhangpo) is a specific kinship term; it may refer more broadly to senior male relatives on the mother's side. The precise social relationship is not entirely clear from context, but "maternal uncles" is the most natural reading.  The name rendered as "Sudarśanā" continues from the preceding passage. The Tibetan "བཟང་མོ" (literally "the good/beautiful one") is used throughout as her name or epithet; it corresponds to Sudarśanā established in the prior context, and is here rendered consistently as such.

The wife's name "འོད་བཟང་མ" literally means "she of beautiful light" and is here rendered as "Prabhāvatī" with the Tibetan gloss provided in parentheses for listener clarity, as this is her first named introduction.

The phrase "teaches the Dharma by body, not by word" is a standard formula for pratyekabuddhas in canonical Vinaya narrative literature, indicating they demonstrate the Dharma through miraculous displays rather than verbal exposition.  The phrase rendered as "dangerous and treacherous resting place" translates གདུག་པ་མང་པོ་ཅན་གྱི་གནས་མལ, literally "a resting place with many harmful things," which in the Vinaya context refers to a place of moral and physical danger, particularly where improper conduct could occur or be alleged. The term གདུག་པ is broader than "dangerous" alone, encompassing malice, harm, and treachery.

The disease name འབྲས ("the fruit of wrong food and conduct") is a Tibetan rendering of a condition associated with dietary or behavioral impropriety; the precise Sanskrit equivalent is uncertain in this context.  The proper name rendered "Viśākhā" appears in the Tibetan as "རྒྱལ་རིགས་དབྱར་ཚུལ་མ," which is an unusual formulation; the identification with Viśākhā (a famous lay devotee at Śrāvastī) is plausible from context and parallel Vinaya accounts, though the Tibetan phrase is not a standard rendering of that name. Similarly, "ཕྱ་མཁན་དྲང་སྲོང་བྱིན" is rendered as "the brahmin ascetic Dīrghanakha," which is a conjecture based on context; the Tibetan may refer to a different figure. The name "རི་དགས་འཛིན་གྱི་མ་ས་ག" is rendered as "the mother of Mṛgāra," following the well-known identification of Viśākhā as "Mṛgāramātā," though the Tibetan phrasing suggests this may be a distinct person listed alongside her.  The passage about "those with black bowls" is an idiomatic reference to non-Buddhist wanderers who carried black begging bowls, distinguishing them from Buddhist monks. The Venerable Ānanda worries this green-haired being might fall into their hands rather than be properly ordained in the Dharma. This is a standard narrative motif in Vinaya literature.

The phrase rendered "deer do not feed deer" is a proverbial expression meaning that fellow monastics are not obliged to support one another materially; each monk must sustain himself through his own alms-round.

The "Group of Six monks" are a notorious group repeatedly referenced in Vinaya literature as exemplars of misconduct, whose bad behavior prompts the Buddha to establish new rules of discipline.  The verse catalogue of physical disqualifications for ordination is a standard Vinaya list; the renderings of anatomical and pathological terms follow the most defensible readings, though several Tibetan terms for specific conditions (notably མཛེ་, འབྲས་, ཕོལ་མིག་, གཏའ་གམ་, ཤུ་བ་, གྱེན་པ་) admit some latitude in precise medical identification. The rendering of ཤ་མདོག་ཁ་དོག་བཞི་པ as "the fourth colour" reflects the Vinaya tradition of four recognized skin tones, with the fourth being an inauspicious or aberrant hue; this is left deliberately literal as the precise referent is a matter of commentarial tradition. The passage ends mid-sentence, as the source text breaks off.  The passage contains a Vinaya narrative in mixed verse and prose typical of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya. The term rendered "kept woman" translates སྐྱོང་བ, meaning a woman maintained as a concubine or ward; "pledged woman" translates གཏའ་གམ, a woman given as a surety or pledge. The term སྲིན་བུ་རི rendered "a mountain of worms" in the summary verse is cryptic and likely refers to a case-narrative heading in the original compendium; its precise referent is uncertain. The passage ends mid-sentence in the source, so the translation ends correspondingly.  The six teachers named here are the classical "six heterodox teachers" (Skt. ṣaṭ śāstāraḥ) of the Pāli and Sanskrit Buddhist tradition: Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Maskarin Gośāla (here "son of the dark-roaming god Kāḷa" renders ཀུན་ཏུ་རྒྱུ་གནག་ལྷས་ཀྱི་བུ, a somewhat literal Tibetan rendering of Maskarin Gośāla's name and epithet), Sañjaya Vairatīputra ( སྨྲ་འདོད་ཀྱི་བུ་མོའི་བུ་ཡང་དག་རྒྱལ་བ་ཅན), Ajita Keśakambala (མི་ཕམ་སྐྲའི་ལ་བ་ཅན), Kakuda Kātyāyana (ཀ་ཏྱའི་བུ་ནོག་ཅན), and Nirgrantha Jñātaputra (གཉེན་གྱི་བུ་གཅེར་བུ་པ, rendered as "Nirgrantha's son" — Nirgrantha Jñātaputra, i.e., Mahāvīra). The Tibetan epithets are literal translations of the names as found in Pāli and Sanskrit sources.  The epithet "Bimbisāra the artisan — Śreṇya" renders the Tibetan "bzo sbyaṅs gzugs can sñiṅ po," which is a Tibetan transcription-rendering of the king's name and epithets. "Gzugs can sñiṅ po" is Bimbisāra and "bzo sbyaṅs" corresponds to Śreṇya or Seniya, a well-known epithet of the Magadhan king; some editions differ in the ordering.

The phrase rendered "the Nirgrantha's son" at the opening corresponds to the series of six non-Buddhist teachers being impersonated; this continues the list from the preceding passage. The Tibetan reads "gcer bu pa gñen gyi bu," meaning the son of the Nirgrantha (i.e., the naked ascetic Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta's tradition), consistent with the continuation of the earlier list.  The term rendered "bystander" or "one who stands apart" for གཟུ་བོ་ལྟ་བུ་ translates a Tibetan expression meaning something like "one who watches from the sidelines" or "an uninvolved onlooker" — the implication being that Prasenajit, unlike the partisan Bimbisāra, might be a more neutral or susceptible audience for their challenge. The precise nuance is contextually inferred.  The phrase rendered "confess wrongdoing and be purified of it" translates a terse construction meaning literally "accumulate evil deeds and then acknowledge them" — the classical idiom for formal confession leading to purification, which is the standard doctrinal sense here.

The "empowerment as regents" renders a phrase in which hearers who have accumulated wholesome roots are given a kind of authorization or investiture to act as stand-ins or deputies of the buddha; this is a specific technical concept within the sūtra's own framing and the rendering follows the literal sense while preserving the doctrinal strangeness.

"Kuśa" as the city name is what the Tibetan spells; this may correspond to another city name in a Sanskrit Vorlage, but the Tibetan is consistent and is rendered as given.  The name "Nagnaja" is a reconstructed Sanskrit equivalent of the Tibetan "na gu" (likely གཞོན་ནུ་ན་གུ), which may mean "the naked-born" or similar. The Tibetan is not entirely transparent here and the exact identity of this prince is uncertain.

The phrase rendered "the great lake Anavatapta" corresponds to མཚོ་ཆེན་པོ་མ་དྲོས་པ, a legendary lake in the Himalayas associated in Buddhist cosmology with cool, pure waters and inhabited by the nāga king Anavatapta. The compound "Anavatapta" is not spelled out in Tibetan but is the standard Sanskrit identification.  The passage contains a formal "truth declaration" or act of truth, a well-attested Indian literary and religious device in which a solemn assertion of a known truth is held to have miraculous efficacy. The Tibetan term rendered here as "truth declaration" is bden pa'i tshig, literally "words of truth." The Blessed One's injunction constitutes a hierarchical enumeration of the Three Jewels and their respective supremacies as the content of the declaration. The phrase rendered "the noble Vinaya in which the noble ones delight" translates 'phags pa dgyes pa'i tshul khrims, a slightly unusual formulation; it refers to the monastic code as cherished or rejoiced in by the noble ones, functioning here as the supreme among those who abide in ethical conduct.  The name of the grove formed from the prince's story presents a minor textual-etymological point. The Tibetan reads "Khaṇḍa-Ānandavana" — a grove named after the episode of the scattered and rejoined limbs, rendered here as "Grove of Rejoining" to make the origin of the name clear to a listening audience. The stone or gem rendered "andara crystal" is uncertain; it appears to be a transliteration of a Sanskrit gem-name not easily identified; this rendering is provisional.  The passage identifies the one who conjures the mango tree as "Cullapanthaka of the Jeta Grove" — the Tibetan reads "dum bu'i kun dga' ra ba pa," literally "the one of the joyful grove of the grove." This is a somewhat compressed epithet; the figure is likely Cullapanthaka (Cūḍapanthaka), a disciple associated with the Jeta Grove, though the precise referent of this name-form in the Tibetan merits verification against the Sanskrit or Chinese parallel. The householder rendered as Anāthapiṇḍika corresponds to the Tibetan "ngan legs sbyin," which is a standard Tibetan rendering of that name.  The names Vimalā, Yārtsulma, Jyin, Nyingpa, and Migdak Dré'i Masa are Tibetan phonetic renderings of Indian names that are difficult to identify with certainty from the Tibetan alone; they are rendered here as transliterations of their Tibetan forms. Anāthapiṇḍada is the standard Sanskrit restoration of the householder whose name literally means "giver of food to the destitute," well attested in the sources.

The kurandaka and kunda are flowering plants and the campaka a fragrant tree, all well known in Sanskrit literary and Buddhist contexts as symbols of beauty and purity.

The final sentence of the passage is syntactically incomplete in the source, ending in a list of qualifiers without a main verb; the translation renders it accordingly, leaving it open as the passage does.  The phrase "the fifth part of the wheel of saṃsāra — its moving and its still" renders a condensed technical expression referring to the five constituents or sections of saṃsāric existence, described through the pair of moving and unmoving phenomena. The precise doctrinal referent is somewhat unusual and may reflect a specific Vinaya or Abhidharma enumeration that the commentarial tradition would clarify; the rendering follows the literal Tibetan closely. The laywoman's name is left in transliterated Tibetan as it appears in the source; a Sanskrit equivalent is not established from context alone.  The names of the novice monk and novice nun rendered here are Kulabhadra and Amogha, the expected Sanskrit behind the Tibetan སྐུལ་བྱེད and བརྗེད་མེད respectively. This is noted but does not affect the doctrinal content.  The phrase rendered "the thirty-second fascicle of the Minor Bases of Discipline" is a section colophon within the Vinaya text (Kṣudrakavastu) marking the end of a bam-po (fascicle) division; it interrupts the narrative but is part of the canonical text as preserved and is therefore included.

The "twin miracle" (Tibetan: zung gi cho 'phrul) is the classical Buddhist miracle in which fire and water issue simultaneously from different parts of the body, traditionally associated with the Śrāvastī miracle of the Buddha. The fourfold deportment display within the sky (walking, standing, sitting, lying) preceding the twin miracle is also a standard element of this narrative.

The word rendered "worldly intention" versus "supramundane intention" translates 'jig rten pa'i thugs bskyed pa and 'jig rten las 'das pa'i thugs bskyed pa respectively. The doctrinal point is that a buddha's ordinary or accessible mental acts can be perceived even by insects through the buddha's mind-radiance, whereas his transcendent, supramundane cognitive acts surpass even the comprehension of arhats.  The verse rendering "logicians" for རྟོག་གེ་ཅན translates a term meaning those who rely on logical reasoning or speculation, often used to refer to Brahmanical or non-Buddhist dialecticians, whose intellectual light is shown to be eclipsed by the Buddha's appearance — a classic polemical image.

The phrase འདམ་བུའི་ཁྱིམ་ལ་གླང་ཆེན་བཞིན translates as "like a great elephant at a house of reeds," which is a standard simile for unstoppable, crushing force — the elephant effortlessly demolishing the fragile dwelling.  The chain of passing the challenge — Pūraṇa Kassapa to Kṛṣṇadeva's son to Vijayaputra and so on — follows a well-known sequence of the six non-Buddhist teachers (the ṣaṭ-śāstṛs) of the Buddha's era. The Tibetan names are rendered as close phonetic equivalents of their standard Sanskrit identifications: Pūraṇa Kassapa, Ajita Keśakambala's disciple, Kātyāyanī's son (Pakudha Kaccāyana), and the naked ascetic Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta's disciple. The precise one-to-one mapping in this particular list is slightly irregular compared to the canonical six, so the identifications follow the Tibetan as given rather than forcing a canonical list.  The term rendered "eunuch" translates མ་ནིང (ma ning), a person of indeterminate or third gender in Indian classificatory thought; "eunuch" is the traditional Tibetan Buddhist commentarial rendering, though some scholars prefer "hermaphrodite" or "third-gender person." The choice here follows classical usage without interrupting the text.

The verse exchange is a rare dramatic interlude; the identity of the young woman in the second exchange is left ambiguous in the Tibetan, likely a female renunciant or ascetic given her Dharma robe.  The epithet rendered "King Vaishravana" translates the Tibetan rgyal po rnam thos bu, which is the standard Tibetan for Vaiśravaṇa, one of the four great guardian kings, associated with the north, wealth, and yakṣas. This is consistent with the narrative context of mass suicide by drowning.  The phrase rendered "means of succession" or "means of kingship" translates a term that in context refers to the formal investiture or regency authority granted to a prince or heir — the political mechanism by which a nephew would be made heir apparent or regent. The name "Rgyal-srid-la-Mngon-par-dga'-ba" is rendered in its full translated form throughout ("Rejoicing-in-the-Royal-Throne") as a story-name whose meaning is plot-significant. The name "Bzabtung" (spelled bza' btung in Tibetan, literally "food and drink") is a narrative proper name used consistently in this text. The phrase rendered "the lord of men follows the way of his kind" translates mi dbang rigs rjes 'gro ba'i rtags yin no — literally "it is the sign that the sovereign of men goes following his lineage/nature," meaning that even the mightiest of men are subject to the alternation of fortune. The passage ends mid-sentence with "the king of the five territories reflected —" because the Tibetan breaks off at that point, clearly continuing in the next section. The Tibetan is somewhat elliptical here, but context makes this the only coherent reading.

The idiom "sounding out the mother's own feelings" translates a compressed Tibetan phrase about taking the warmth of the mother's sentiment — a colloquial expression for gauging how someone truly feels before acting.  The names Bha-tung and Bha-tung Mangpo appear to be transcriptions of indigenous (likely non-Sanskrit, possibly Old Tibetan or regional) names meaning something like "Eater" and "Great Eater" or "Much-Eater." The epithet "Vaiśravaṇa's son" in the verse addressed to Gangpo is puzzling, as Gangpo is a village headman, not Vaiśravaṇa. The Tibetan reads "rnam thos bu," literally "son of Vaiśravaṇa." The place name "Apaṇajarī" renders the Tibetan "ཨ་པ་ཛ་རི" as a phonetic transcription of what is likely a Sanskrit toponym associated with Sāṃkāśya (the traditional site of the Buddha's descent from Tuṣita — here rendered as the Thirty-Three Gods' realm, which is Trāyastriṃśa). The passage states the Blessed One taught the Dharma in the Yāma heavens on his way down — this downward sequence through the divine realms is a standard narrative element of the Sāṃkāśya descent story found in Vinaya and other sources.  The sequence of heavenly realms listed here follows the standard Abhidharma cosmology of the form realm: the three Brahmic heavens, three radiance heavens, three virtue heavens, and the five Pure Abodes capped by Akaniṣṭha, which the Blessed One visits in descending reverse order. The text's unusual feature of having him descend from Akaniṣṭha downward through the realms — rather than simply descending from the Thirty-Three — is preserved faithfully.

The name "Sarvārthasiddha" (lhas bcu cad dang ldan pa, literally "endowed with all purposes" or "accomplishing all aims") is the same name as Siddhārtha in its fuller form; here it refers to a divine youth in the assembly, not the bodhisattva who became the Buddha.

The phrase rendered "vomit warm blood and die on the spot" reflects a classical Indian literary idiom for death from overwhelming shock or overpowering splendor, attested in other sūtra contexts. The translation renders accordingly.

The phrase rendered "six rules and the six rules that accompany them" refers to the śikṣamāṇā (probationary nun) training: six primary rules and six secondary or attendant rules to be kept for two years before full ordination. The name "Skaṃmā Gautamī" renders སྐེམ་མོ་གཽ་ཏ་མཱི, which corresponds to Sanskrit Kṣemā Gautamī or possibly Śyāmā Gautamī. The first syllable སྐེམ་མོ is uncertain; it may be a Tibetan phonetic rendering of a Sanskrit name not easily recoverable from this form alone. This is consequential because it identifies a specific nun.

The phrase འཕགས་མ་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་རྣམས་ནི་གཟུང་བར་དཀའ་སྟེ is somewhat elliptical. Rendered here as "afflictions are difficult to restrain," it could also mean "noble ones are difficult to grasp or take hold of" — the doctrinal point being that the afflictions seize women in ways that are hard to check. The translation follows the contextual sense of the women's petition to the nun for guidance.  The phrase rendered "submit yourselves to my authority" translates a construction meaning literally "offer the law to me" or "hand authority over to me," which in context means placing themselves under Sthūlanandā's direction or management — a euphemism for her acting as a procuress. The translation conveys this pragmatic meaning without editorializing.

The closing reference to "one who has eaten the flesh of her own child" alludes to a canonical story, likely the tale of Kuntī or a similar narrative of extreme suffering due to famine or karmic consequence, which the text is about to recount. No textual corruption is suspected; the allusion is left to context.  The phrase rendered "twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection" is a standard Abhidharma metaphor: the twenty-peak mountain represents the twenty modes of the view of self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), comprising the fivefold attribution of self and mine to each of the five aggregates. The image of the vajra of primordial wisdom shattering these peaks signals the attainment of stream-entry (srotāpatti), which cuts the fetter of the view of the transitory collection entirely.

The verse stanza near the middle of the passage is terse and possibly mnemonic in character; "cross-legged sitting is without category" renders a phrase that may mean the rule about sitting cross-legged in the presence of a monk has no enumerated exception — a minor point of Vinaya procedure. This reading is defensible but the exact nuance is not certain.  The epithet of Bhomā rendered "master of the Three Baskets" translates the Tibetan phrase indicating she claims command of the Tripiṭaka, used here with clear irony given the context of her arrogance. The phrase "fool upon fool, dullard upon dullard" renders a double intensification in the Tibetan, indicating degrees of stupidity.  The phrase rendered "what is called the wound that is womanhood" reflects a difficult and anatomically crude expression in the Vinaya literature. The Tibetan "བུད་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བའི་རྨའི་སྒོར་སྲོག་ཆགས་དག་ཞུགས་པར" literally means "creatures entered into the opening of the wound called woman." This is an archaic Vinaya idiom, likely reflecting a canonical Indian view of the female body; the rendering preserves it faithfully without softening.

The phrase rendered "half cross-legged on a mat" for "སྐྱིལ་མོ་ཀྲུང་ཕྱེད་དུ་ཆོས་ལ་འདུག་པས" involves some interpretive difficulty. The compound "ཆོས་ལ་འདུག་པ" could mean "sitting in the proper or lawful manner" or "sitting in accordance with the rule." The translation "in the proper manner" is chosen to capture both the posture and the Vinaya connotation.  The verse in the middle of the passage presents a compressed, aphoristic quality. The phrase rendered "the flow of blood" for "khrag 'dzag pa" is a standard Vinaya idiom indicating menstruation, contextually used to mark the specific restrictions applicable to nuns; the verse as a whole appears to be a mnemonic summarizing the rules just discussed regarding what a monk will not forgo and what a nun may not inquire about.  The verse quatrain near the end is terse and the Tibetan is somewhat compressed. The rendering "unclean" refers to menstrual or parturition blood; "nursing-cloth" and "nursing-band" render ནུ་རྟེན and ནུ་མཆིངས, terms for garments or supports used in breastfeeding or postpartum care. The precise referents of these Vinaya technical terms are debated in the commentarial tradition, and the translation renders the plain sense.

The epithet Gautamī for Mahāprajāpatī (here གཽ་ཏ་མཱི་སྐྱེ་དགུའི་བདག་མོ་ཆེན་མོ) is her clan name; "mother of the people" renders སྐྱེ་དགུའི་བདག་མོ་ཆེན་མོ literally, though it is also an honorific epithet for Mahāprajāpatī as foster-mother of the Buddha.  The phrase rendered "monk her father in the Dharma" translates the Tibetan literally: the monk is the nun's senior male counterpart in the Vinaya relationship, here expressed as "father monk" (dge slong pha). This is a standard Vinaya category denoting a senior monk in a quasi-parental disciplinary relationship to a nun.

The name Sthūlanandā is the standard Sanskrit reconstruction for the Tibetan "Sbom dga' mo" (meaning "Fat Joyful One"). The queen's name Mālagandha (Tibetan: phreng ldan ma, "Garland-fragrant") is reconstructed on the same basis.  The three garments in this passage present a terminological sequence: the waist-cincher (Tib. rkyed chings), the breast-band (nu rten), and the breast-support or breast-separator (nu ma'i bar chad, literally "that which occupies the interval between the breasts," likely a garment that lifts or separates the breasts). The distinctions among these three items are clear in the Tibetan and have been rendered accordingly. The Vinaya narrative follows a formulaic pattern in which the same episode is repeated with a new garment each time; the translation preserves that repetitive structure deliberately, as it reflects the canonical form of rule-origination stories.  The verse summary in this passage is a mnemonic tag condensing the preceding rules into shorthand. The line rendered as "Do not discard it in an unclean place — the womb, impurity, and foul drink" is terse and deliberately abbreviated; the full legal content is in the narrative prose around it. The reference to "the womb" alludes to the rule about not discarding waste in a womb-related place, while "foul drink" likely points to a separate rule not yet fully narrated at this point in the text.

The phrase rendered as "the one dwelling in my womb" translates the Tibetan term for a being already conceived, making clear the child was still in utero when the decision to abort was made. The narrative is heading toward a rule about a nun acting as an abortionist, a serious transgression in the Vinaya literature.  The phrase rendered "she rebuked him eight times" translates a Tibetan idiom for a strong, emphatic rebuke; the number eight here likely reflects a formulaic expression of repeated insistence rather than a literal count of eight utterances.

The name Guptā renders the Tibetan "གུབ་ཏས," and young Kāśyapa renders "གཞོན་ནུ་འོད་སྲུང." The story of Kāśyapa's miraculous conception from a drop of urine, without physical contact, is a well-known narrative in Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya literature.

The closing verse summary is a colophon-style mnemonic listing topics covered in or adjacent to this section of the Vinaya; the rendering attempts to follow the compressed, list-like Tibetan closely, though the final lines are deliberately terse in the original.  The phrase rendered "Rādha" at the opening refers to the same Rādha mentioned in the immediately preceding passage; the text here is a brief verse-like summary line indicating that the rules just stated apply equally to boys, girls, novices, and Rādha. The name "Guptā" renders Tibetan "Gub ta" and the boy's name "Kāśyapa" renders "Od srung gzhon nu" (literally "young Kāśyapa / young Protector of Light"), a standard Tibetan rendering of the Sanskrit name Kāśyapa meaning "one who protects brilliance."  The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end, rendering the final passage about the two generations incomplete. The phrase "གྲོགས་པོ་ཡུ་བུ་གཉིས་དུས་ལས་འདས་ཀྱང་" is somewhat elliptical. The exact syntactic completion of this sentence depends on the continuation of the passage.

The name rendered "Guptā" follows the established rendering from the preceding passage. The epithet "Kāśyapa the Elder" renders "འོད་སྲུང་ཆེན་པོ," literally "great Kāśyapa," and refers to Mahākāśyapa, one of the principal disciples of the Buddha. The identification of the son as Mahākāśyapa is an unusual hagiographical detail preserved in this Vinaya narrative context.  The name Joymaker renders the Tibetan "Dga' byed ma," a feminine name meaning "she who makes joy" or "she who causes delight" — a transparent formation chosen to reflect the narrative etymology given in the text. The boy's name Pāñcika is a Sanskrit patronymic from Pañcāla, and is kept in its Sanskrit form as it becomes a proper name in the tradition. The crane cry at the moment of conception and birth is a folk-omen motif whose significance will presumably be developed in the narrative that follows.  The name Sātakiri is a compound formed from Sāta (the father's name) and giri (mountain), yielding something like "Sāta-of-the-mountain" or "Mountain-Sāta," reflecting the text's own folk etymology linking the father's name and the crane's cry from the mountain. The Tibetan ས་ཏ་གི་རི literally renders this compound.

The yakṣa Pañcāla and the young yakṣa Pāñcika appear to be distinct figures: Pañcāla is the elder to whom the earlier betrothal was made, while Pāñcika is the young yakṣa to whom Pañcāla gives Joymaker in marriage. This distinction is maintained in the translation.  The phrase rendered "the Blessed One granted permission by his silence" follows the standard canonical idiom in which a Tathāgata's silence in response to a request constitutes assent; this is a well-established convention in Vinaya and sūtra narrative literature and requires no special comment beyond noting the deliberate wordlessness.  The names of the hell realms listed follow the standard Sanskrit series: Sañjīva, Kāḷasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci (the eight hot hells), followed by the cold hells Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma. The Tibetan here renders most of these by translation or partial transcription; the Sanskrit names are restored for clarity.

The child's name, rendered here as "Joymaker," translates the Tibetan Dga' byed, which corresponds to Sanskrit Priyaṃkara or a similar form meaning "one who makes delight."

Maṇibhadra is identified here as the lord of the yakṣas (gnod sbyin gyi bdag po ngal bso po); the epithet ngal bso po, meaning "the one who gives rest" or "the refresher," is a standard Tibetan rendering of Maṇibhadra's name and function.  The yakṣinī's name, rendered in the preceding passage as "Aprāptā" (from Tibetan འཕྲོག་མ), literally means "she who seizes" or "snatching-one." The speech by Maṇibhadra identifies the "chieftain" (སྡེ་དཔོན་, sde dpon) as the ascetic Gautama — meaning the Buddha — which is an unusual construction in which Aprāptā herself seems to name Gautama as the chieftain she has been told about, or Maṇibhadra identifies Gautama as the chieftain who can help. The syntax is somewhat compressed in the original, and the reading adopted here is the most coherent one.  The phrase rendered "in the end, a single worldly benefactor with warm devotion" translates a compressed and difficult clause. The Tibetan reads literally something like "because compassion dwells toward the weak and lowly, in the end a single worldly donor of heat." The precise sense is obscure; this rendering reflects the most plausible reading — that the pratyekabuddha accepts alms from humble donors out of compassion — but the clause is genuinely difficult and may be corrupt or elliptical.  The term saṃkakṣikā refers to a half-garment or underrobe covering the torso and upper arms, worn during physical work or bathing to preserve decency. The Tibetan transliteration is preserved throughout the passage as a technical Vinaya term without a fully transparent Tibetan rendering.

The phrase rendered as "others of different faith mocked them" translates a brief clause indicating that those who were not followers of the Buddha took the opportunity to ridicule the nuns — a stock Vinaya scenario contrasting the reactions of the laypeople who became attached with those who expressed disapproval.  The term rendered "person with two sex characteristics" translates a technical Vinaya category referring to individuals with ambiguous or combined sexual anatomy, in Sanskrit pandaka or ubhayavyañjanaka depending on the specific context. Here the Tibetan uses a term literally meaning "one having two marks/signs," which corresponds most precisely to ubhayavyañjanaka in the broader Vinaya taxonomy of those excluded from ordination. The category "hermaphrodite" is used as the closest conventional rendering, though the Vinaya taxonomy is more nuanced than any single modern term captures.

The verse summarizes four categories of persons ineligible for ordination that the surrounding narrative sections address: those with two sex characteristics, those whose passages are blocked, those who always discharge blood, and those who have no menstrual blood at all. The final category, one with no blood, is introduced in the verse but its narrative case is not yet rendered here, as the source passage ends before it.

The phrase rendered "stopped up" or "whose passages were blocked" refers to a physiological condition in which urinary and intestinal passages are abnormally connected or obstructed, causing involuntary simultaneous evacuation.  The verse passage in the middle of this text is terse and somewhat cryptic. The rendering "the gesture of spitting" for ཐུ་མི་བྱ is based on the Vinaya context where spitting (or making a gesture of contempt or dismissal) is a recognized ceremonial act; the exact referent may be a specific ritual gesture of reception or rejection in the ordination procedure. The line དགེ་སློང་འཆགས meaning "take on the form of a monk" is interpretive; it may refer to a hermaphrodite adopting monks' robes or status. The figure ཞིང་དགའ་མོ་བསོད་སྙོམས་ is rendered as "the joyful Nandā" following the standard identification of this stock character in Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya narrative.  The term rendered "Pom-delight" follows the preceding passage's established rendering of སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ. The phrase "monk who is her monastic father" renders དགེ་སློང་ཕ, literally "monk-father," a recognized Vinaya term for the monk under whose authority or in relation to whom a nun stands in a particular institutional relationship; the precise technical meaning of this term as the passage continues would benefit from seeing the following sentence, which is where the ruling is completed.  The phrase rendered "communal acts" translates སྤྱི་ལས, meaning acts that are held jointly between the two communities rather than separately by each order. The figure translated as "great lay patroness" renders སྐྱེ་དགུའི་བདག་མོ་ཆེན་མོ, literally "great mistress of beings" — a title for a prominent lay female donor or patroness of high social standing.

The final verse lines are the closing summary verse of a Vinaya section; the last line ("one should not strike a person with a harmful garment or the chest") is terse and likely refers to rules against using clothing or physical contact as forms of assault or inappropriate touching — the precise referent is unclear without the fuller Vinaya context.  The phrase rendered "an offense with expiation" translates a standard Vinaya term for a pācittiya-class transgression, meaning a downfall that requires confession and expiation before the community but does not constitute a root defeat. The text does not spell out the Tibetan term in full here but it is implied by the formula "འདས་པ་དང་བཅས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ," which in Vinaya contexts consistently marks this category of offense.

The name "Sthūlanandā" is the Sanskrit reconstruction of the Tibetan སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ, literally "Fat Joyful One," a well-known nun in the Vinaya narratives notorious for misconduct.  The phrase rendered "sons of that slave woman" translates a Tibetan insult directed at the king's men. The phrase rendered "a man to act as a pimp" translates a term literally meaning "a man who guards or watches" in the context of the sex trade; the rendering is a contextual interpretation consistent with the narrative logic. The passage lists the attainments of the audience using the standard Abhidharmic scheme of the four fruits of the śrāvaka path: stream-entry (Skt. srotāpatti), once-returning (Skt. sakṛdāgāmin), non-returning (Skt. anāgāmin), and arhathood.
