Some editions may read this differently.

The name གྲེ་ལས་སྐྱེས (Grelaskyé) is a Tibetan transcription of a Sanskrit proper name that cannot be securely reconstructed without access to a parallel Sanskrit recension. It appears to be a monk whose remains are honored by the twelve nuns.

The phrase དུས་ལས་འདས་པ ("passed beyond his time") is a standard Tibetan euphemism for death, rendered here as "passed away."  The name "Chutung" appears to be a Tibetan rendering of a proper name (literally meaning "water-drinker"), which was also used in the preceding passage as the name of the venerable elder arriving with five hundred monks. The text is consistent in using this name, and it is preserved as such for continuity with the previous rendering.

The expression translated as "she blessed her robe through her power of concentration" renders a compact phrase indicating that Utpalavarnā used her supernormal ability to imbue her robe with a protective quality before entering the absorption of cessation. The precise mechanism is left elliptical in the Tibetan.  The passage ends mid-sentence in the Tibetan as given, breaking off at the conditional clause about what happens if a nun enters without having been asked. The translation reflects this open ending faithfully.

The epithet སྐྱེ་དགུའི་བདག་མོ་ཆེན་མོ, literally "great mistress of beings," is a standard Tibetan rendering of the Sanskrit Mahāprajāpatī, the name of the Buddha's aunt and the first Buddhist nun. It has been rendered accordingly.  The summary verse is a mnemonic gāthā condensing the preceding legal rulings on the poṣadha and pravāraṇā ceremonies and the procedure for nuns seeking consent. The verse's compressed syntax follows standard Vinaya mnemonic style.

The term rendered "gradually" (Tibetan: bgags kyis) in the forgiveness procedure is a procedural term indicating a staged or mediated reconciliation rather than an immediate, direct confrontation — a nuance preserved in the translation.  The passage contains a characteristically repetitive Vinaya-style enumeration of the three unwholesome and three wholesome roots, repeated in slightly varying formulations as part of an oral-formulaic structure. The text appears to break off mid-sentence at the end; the translation renders what is present in the passage without supplying missing text.

The phrase rendered "acts of aggression" translates a cluster of terms including fighting, fault-finding, abuse, quarreling, and a fifth term suggesting aggressive confrontation or incitement; these have been rendered as a unified list throughout for naturalness in speech.  The term rendered "invitation ceremony" throughout is the Pravāraṇā, the formal ceremony at the end of the rains retreat in which monastics invite correction from their fellows. The term rendered "Restoration" in the final section is Poṣadha, the fortnightly confession and recitation of the Prātimokṣa; both terms appear in the house glossary and are used consistently.

The phrase "recover his own mind of renunciation" renders the Tibetan idiom for the re-establishing of each individual's proper monastic resolve or composure after conflict — literally "separately obtaining his mind of renunciation." The rendering is interpretive but doctrinal.

The "topknot festival" is a calendrical observance whose exact identification in this Vinaya context is uncertain; it may refer to a specific Indian festival associated with hair-offering rites.  The phrase rendered as "shaven-headed nuns" and "shaven-headed wanderers" translates the Tibetan terms for nuns and monastics in the mouths of the brahmins and householders, who use the colloquial derogatory expression for shaven-headed renunciants. The scornful tone is deliberate and belongs to the speakers, not to the text itself.

The final line, "Here ends the summary verse," renders the Tibetan closing marker indicating that a mnemonic summary verse follows, though the verse itself does not appear in this passage.  The phrase rendered as "the five-spoked wheel of a vehicle" reflects a somewhat unusual image in this narrative context; the Tibetan reads "sgo khang na 'khor ba'i 'khor lo cha lnga pa la rtog cing 'dug go," which literally means he sat in the gatehouse examining a five-part or five-spoked wheel. This detail appears to be a narrative flourish establishing that the man is a wandering craftsman or trader, not a monk, and the translation follows the literal reading. Some commentators may read 'khor ba here differently, but the sense of a wheeled conveyance or cartwheel seems most natural in context.  The phrase rendered "turning the wheel of cyclic existence in his mind" translates the idiom for a non-monk lay person sitting in a gatehouse being preoccupied with worldly affairs — the nuns described him only by his appearance and posture, not knowing he was a layman. The "wheel of cyclic existence" here is a vivid way of characterizing his mental state as worldly, not a technical Dharma usage.

The title "Great Progenitress" for Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī renders སྐྱེ་དགུའི་བདག་མོ་ཆེན་མོ་གཽ་ཏ་མཱི, where སྐྱེ་དགུའི་བདག་མོ means "mistress of beings" or "progenitress of beings," an honorific for Mahāprajāpatī. The passage alternates between her full title and the shorter གཽ་ཏ་མཱི alone.  The phrase rendered "My good woman, I know how. Since the time has passed, there is not a craft or a trade I do not know" is somewhat compressed in the Tibetan. The speaker is Sthūlanandā boasting of her skills; the sense is that over time she has come to know every craft and trade, and the translation reflects that confident self-assertion.  The list of named individuals in the festival passage is slightly compressed in the Tibetan and some names are abbreviated or variant forms. "Queen Mallikā" renders བཙུན་མོ་ཕྲེང་ལྡན་མ, literally "Queen Garland-Bearer," which is a standard Tibetan rendering of Mallikā. "Vāsavadattā" renders རྒྱལ་རིགས་དབྱར་བྱེད་མ, a royal lady whose name is uncertain from this epithet alone; the rendering is tentative. The passage ends mid-sentence in the source text, reflecting an abrupt cut in the supplied Tibetan.  The phrase rendered "born laterally on the right side" translates a compound indicating an oblique or lateral birth position on the right side, understood in the narrative as an inauspicious birth sign. The exact medical or cultural referent is not further specified in the text.

The nested-bowl episode involves Sthūlanandā commissioning progressively smaller bowls that nest inside one another; the text's phrasing is somewhat compressed but the sense of a graduated set of seven nesting bowls is clear from context.  The final two sentences mark a sharp transition to a formulaic legal declaration within the Vinaya narrative frame. The phrase rendered "the fully ordained nuns of the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, are burned — the brahmin life is burned" reflects the stock Vinaya expression used when a monk or nun has committed a breach: "burned" here means their celibate religious life has been compromised or violated. The term "brahmin life" renders tshangs par spyod pa, literally "pure conduct" or "brahmic conduct," the standard term for the celibate religious life (Sanskrit brahmacaryā). The passage signals that a Vinaya offense is being narrated.  The phrase rendered "praised me to the skies like an elephant's raised trunk" is an idiomatic Tibetan expression of flattery or grand proclamation; the simile of the elephant's uplifted trunk conveys lofty, public praise. The rendering preserves the figurative sense for a listening audience.

The repeated narrative frame, "The brahmin life was burned" and "the contemplatives, the sons of the Śākyas, were burned," is a formulaic Vinaya expression indicating that the reputation and good name of the monastic community was damaged or inflamed by public scandal.  The phrase rendered "Stubborn Delightful" translates the nun's name སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ (Stubborn-Joyful or Obstinate Delight); it is preserved consistently from the preceding passage. The signal she gives indicating "the female donor had but little gain" is a somewhat compressed idiom; the Tibetan མཚན་མ་ཞིག་ཉེ་བར་བསྟན་པ refers to her making a sign or giving a hint — the precise nature of the sign is not specified in the text.  The summary verse appears to be a mnemonic listing several Vinaya rules in compressed form. The individual terms are elliptical, and the rendering given follows the most natural reading of each phrase as a rule-heading rather than a complete sentence — this is standard for such verse summaries in Vinaya literature. The phrase rendered "gall-bladder vessel" translates a term for a kind of container; the precise referent is a minor point of Vinaya material culture and is not consequential for the doctrinal content.  The name rendered "Stout-and-Glad" translates the Tibetan "སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ" (Sbom dga' mo), literally "Fat-Joy" or "Stout-Delighted." This is a personal name of a nun and has been rendered in a natural English compound reflecting its literal meaning. Some editions may read this differently.

The phrase "འགལ་ཚབས་ཅན་དུ་འགྱུར་རོ" rendered as "it will be a matter involving an offence" is a Vinaya technical formula; the exact grade of offence is not specified in this passage.

The summary verse at the close is a standard mnemonic (uddāna) marking the end of a section; the four items it enumerates summarize preceding rules. The referent of "these four" is the four cases treated in the preceding section, which is conventional in Vinaya uddāna verses.  The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end ("མ་ཀུན་དག་ཐུ" — literally "all the mothers..."), indicating the supplied Tibetan is incomplete. The translation reflects this abrupt ending faithfully.

The phrase rendered "nocturnal emission" translates "mi gtsang ba yang byung," literally "something unclean also arose/occurred," a standard Vinaya euphemism for seminal or vaginal discharge during sleep; the context makes the meaning clear.

The signal left at the doorway (flour or pickles/condiments) is a standard Vinaya device to indicate prior arrival and avoid entering a household unannounced; "ཚོད་མ" (tshod ma) here likely means condiments or pickled vegetables rather than fresh vegetables, functioning as a recognizable marker.  The term rendered "staff-bell" (Tibetan: khar gsil) corresponds to the Sanskrit khakkhara, the ringed walking staff traditionally carried by monks, which jingles as they walk and can be shaken to announce one's arrival. This is its standard Vinaya identification.

The phrase rendered "a room built up with materials" translates rdzas kyis bsgrubs pa, literally "accomplished or constructed by means of requisites or materials." This is a technical Vinaya designation for a temporary dwelling or cell assembled from donated supplies; the exact nature of the structure is deliberately left in plain descriptive language rather than over-specified.  The passage contains a string of onomatopoeic Tibetan syllables rendered here as approximations in English, since the original clearly intends to evoke the actual sounds of eating and drinking. The precise onomatopoeia differs between languages, but the general sense is preserved. The term translated as "rice-porridge" for འབྲས་ཁུར་ covers a thick rice dish; "porridge" for ཐུག་པ covers a general thick soup or congee. The phrase ནང་དུ་ཡང་དག་འཇོག is rendered as "inner composure," a standard Vinaya idiom for the Buddha's afternoon period of meditative rest.  The phrase rendered "a place prepared with requisites" translates the Tibetan for a dwelling or setting arranged with the four requisites offered to the Buddha; this is a standard Vinaya context indicating the Buddha accepted an invitation and sat within a formally prepared space while also going on alms round, a juxtaposition that the text itself flags as requiring explanation through the "five reasons" passage referenced but not quoted here.  The phrase rendered "occupied with a matter" for རྫས་ཀྱིས་བསྒྲུབས་པ་ན་བཞུགས is a Vinaya technical idiom; it refers to the Blessed One remaining behind to attend to some business or matter rather than going with the assembly. The passage cross-references an earlier section of the Vinaya narrative (the "five reasons" passage) which is not reproduced here; the instruction "as stated above" reflects the Tibetan's own cross-referential shorthand.

The closing summary verse is a mnemonic gāthā listing topics covered in the fascicle; the four items enumerated correspond to four separate narrative sections, of which only the last two appear in this passage.  The phrase rendered "bathing" throughout refers to a therapeutic soaking or irrigation of a wound, not ordinary bathing. The Tibetan verb "khrus byed" normally means to bathe, but in this medical context it describes rinsing or washing a treated wound — the poultice procedure requires the wound to be fully irrigated before rinsing with cold or warm water. The narrative logic makes clear that the problem was applying cold water too soon and only once.

The expression "brahmin endowed with the six qualities" refers to a brahmin of full hereditary qualification according to traditional Indian brahminical reckoning: noble birth on both sides for seven generations, expertise in the Vedas, handsome appearance, good character, learning, and so forth. The specific six qualities vary by source.  The phrase rendered "being of his last existence" translates "srid pa tha ma pa'i sems can," literally "the sentient being of the last existence," a technical term for one whose current life will be their final rebirth before nirvāṇa — here the child who is about to be ordained.

The term rendered "house-cricket" for "srog chags khyim sbyong" is uncertain; the compound could refer to various small domestic insects or vermin. The identity of the creature is not doctrinally significant.  The phrase rendered "wheel of existence, fivefold, moving and unmoving" translates a technical Vinaya formula for the five aggregates or the constituents of conditioned existence; the exact doctrinal referent is somewhat compressed in the Tibetan and may allude to a stock phrase from Abhidharma enumeration. The rendering is faithful to the Tibetan syntax while keeping it intelligible in context.

The phrase "like stone and gold alike" and "like the sky and like the palm of the hand" are stock simile-pairs for an arhat's equanimity, well attested in Vinaya narrative literature; they are rendered literally as the tradition intends them.  The verse "Even were it a hundred aeons..." is a well-known canonical gāthā attested in multiple Āgama and Vinaya sources; it is cited here in the standard form.

The summary verse at the close is a colophon-style mnemonic gāthā listing key narrative elements of the story. The phrase rendered "the one carrying a load who makes no sound, who does not eat" corresponds to the image of the snake (which carried its karmic burden silently), and these compressed summaries are conventional in this genre. The precise referents of each phrase within the mnemonic are intentionally condensed and some ambiguity is inherent to the genre.

The transition after the summary verse marks a new sūtra episode beginning with a fresh setting, which is standard in this collection.  The phrase rendered as "code phrase" translates a term literally meaning something like "a word that conceals" or "a substitute expression," used here in the sense of a veiled or encoded expression, where each ordinary image stands for a doctrinal reality. The rendering "code phrase" is chosen for clarity in a spoken context.

The passage about the monk of little learning and the bandits sets up a narrative of danger in the wilderness — a typical Vinaya illustrative story establishing the context for a subsequent rule.  The phrase rendered as "master of the Three Baskets" refers to one who has mastered the Tripiṭaka. The term མ་མོ་འཛིན་པ, literally "holder of the Mātṛkā," refers to the Abhidharma matrix-texts or numerical summaries; this is an older designation for what became the Abhidharma Piṭaka, rendered here by its Sanskrit technical name to preserve the scholastic sense. The repeated formula "I am a forest-dweller" is the monk's consistent and almost absurdist self-identification, likely conveying either a vow of strict forest renunciation that precluded all social knowledge, or a deliberate meditative refusal of conventional categories; the narrative presents this without irony as the cause of the bandits' outrage.  The term translated as "Mātṛkā" refers to the Abhidharma matrix texts or their proto-forms. It sits alongside Sūtra and Vinaya as the third division of the canon, though in this early Vinaya context it likely refers to summary doctrinal lists rather than the fully developed Abhidharma.

The place name "Anupiya" renders Tibetan "འདོད་པ་མཐུན་པ" three times. This is the standard Tibetan rendering of the toponym Anupiya (also spelled Anupiyā), a town and mango grove near Kapilavāstu associated with early Buddhist narratives. The repeated phrase in the Tibetan is formulaic, establishing arrival at and residence in that locale.

The young brahmin's name "Maṣu" is a tentative rendering of "མ་སྡུག." The name is unclear and may be a Tibetan phonetic rendering of an Indic original not easily recovered.  The passage employs the standard ten epithets of a buddha, here rendered according to their established canonical meanings. The repeated phrase "from home into homelessness" renders the classical going-forth formula. The phrase translated "sacred brahmin formularies" or "secret formularies" renders gsang tshig, literally "secret words," referring to the esoteric Vedic or brahminical texts in which the marks of a great man are said to be described — a detail common to parallel Pāli sūtra passages. The name Maṣu corresponds to the young brahmin introduced as Ma su in the preceding passage.  The phrase rendered "dark-limbed menials born of Brahma's foot" (dge sbyong mgo reg nag po'i rtsa lag pho reng) is a derogatory epithet that the brahmin youth Ambastha appears to be applying to ascetics of low birth, reflecting the Brahmanical varna ideology in which śūdras are said to originate from Brahma's feet. The Blessed One is turning this language back on Ambastha ironically, noting that even with such menials a brahmin does not behave with such rudeness. The syntax here is compressed and the passage is echoing the Ambaṭṭha Sutta (DN 3); the translation follows that context.  The section heading "Vinaya — the Minor Matters. The Forty-Sixth Bundle" appears mid-passage as a Tibetan canonical colophon marker indicating a fascicle division within the Vinaya Kṣudrakavastu; it interrupts the narrative and is rendered plainly as it stands in the source, since it is present in the text.

The name "Icchanangala" renders the Tibetan མིག་མི་འཛུམས་ཀྱི་བུ, literally "son of the Unblinking Eye," which corresponds to the Pāli Icchānangala or, in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta context, a patronymic. The exact Sanskrit form is uncertain; the rendering follows contextual identification with the Pāli tradition's Cankī or related figures, though the Tibetan here is likely a rendering of a name meaning something like "son of the unblinking one."

The four sons' names — Starface, Handear, Tamed by the Elephant, and Ornamented Feet — render Tibetan སྐར་མདའི་གདོང, ལག་རྣ, གླང་པོ་ཆེས་འདུལ་བ, and རྐང་རྒྱན་ལྡན respectively. These correspond to the Pāli Okkāmukha, Karakaṇḍa, Hatthinīka, and Sinipura, though the Tibetan renderings diverge somewhat from the Pāli names; the translation follows the literal Tibetan meaning.  The name "Ngophödma" is a transliteration of a Tibetan rendering of a Pāli name (likely Dishnī or a similar slave woman's name from the Ambaṭṭha Sutta of the Dīgha Nikāya). The Tibetan text gives it as a proper name without further gloss; I have retained the Tibetan form and added the likely Pāli equivalent parenthetically in a light way. The rākṣasa passage is rendered following the Tibetan closely; in the Pāli source this episode concerns the Kaṇhāyana lineage differently, but the Tibetan here reads "Unblinking Ones" as a class of beings equivalent to rākṣasas.

The phrase "splitting the head into seven pieces" is a standard formulaic expression in these sūtra accounts for the consequence of refusing to answer a teacher's question three times.  The fourfold sequence of hypothetical cases about caste-mixing and ritual privilege follows the structure of the Ambaṭṭha Sutta. The term rendered "secret words" renders གསང་ཚིག, which in the Pali corresponds to mantras or sacred formulae transmitted within brahmin lineages. "Seat" and "water" refer to the customary hospitality honours due to qualified brahmins. "Anointing" renders དབང་བསྐུར, literally "empowerment," but here used in the sense of the royal or kṣatriya consecration rite. The figure of King Okkāka and the sage expelled by brahmin penalty appear in the extended narrative context of the sutta; the Tibetan here follows the standard account.  The figure called "the lord of the Mithilā brahmins, Brahmā" renders མི་མཇེད་ཀྱི་བདག་པོ་ཚངས་པ. This is a brahmin named or epithetized Brahmā who is lord of the Mithilā region; the text presents him as a human brahmin lord, not the deity Brahmā. This is consistent with similar passages in related Pāli sūtra literature where a brahmin is compared to or named after Brahmā.

The repeated verse citation, appearing three times in the passage, is a standard rhetorical feature of this type of sūtra dialogue affirming the authority of a verse by attributing it to oneself and to the interlocutor in sequence.  The compound rendered "like the sound of a royal court assembly" translates a phrase that literally suggests speech resembling the resonant sound within a royal palace and its surrounding assembly — conveying a quality of dignified, well-rounded sonic fullness. The rendering captures the simile's intended sense.

The terms for fraudulent commercial practices (falsifying measures of volume, scales, and weights) reflect standard Vinaya and sūtra enumerations of merchant dishonesty.  The phrase rendered as "one who has a light and with a woman" reflects the Tibetan literally: འོད་དང་བུད་མེད་ཅན་དང་ལྷན་ཅིག་ཉལ་བ. The term འོད་ཅན ("one who has a light") is ambiguous and may refer to sleeping in a room with a lamp lit, or alongside a person carrying a light — the exact sense is uncertain and likely reflects a Vinaya-context prohibition against sharing sleeping quarters in these circumstances. This is a genuine exegetical uncertainty worth flagging.

The term ཞོ་ཤས་འཚོ་བ (those who subsist on whey) may be a social category of dependent laborers or bondspeople identified by their meager subsistence.

The passage ends mid-sentence, enumerating types of luxurious furnishings; the translation faithfully follows the text to its terminus.  The passage contains an extended catalogue of games and entertainments that closely parallels the Brahmajāla Sutta list of wrong livelihood. Several terms in the games section are obscure and their exact referents uncertain. "Miig brgyad pa" and "miig bcu pa" likely refer to board games played on eight-square and ten-square grids respectively, analogous to Pali "aṭṭhapada" and "dasapada." "Na ya'i mig" is rendered "the eye of nāya," following a conventional reading but the precise game is unclear. "Gul tshab," rendered "substitution-moves," and "pheg," rendered "bouncing games," are also of uncertain precise meaning. "Rang bzo'i sgra," rendered "the sound of amateur performances," may alternatively refer to improvised or spontaneous sounds. These uncertainties do not affect the doctrinal substance of the passage.  The list of omen-reading and ritual arts in the final two paragraphs presents some cataloguing challenges. The term rendered "momentary conjunctions" translates a compound referring to brief astrological configurations. "Reading of fields" renders a term that could also denote reading of the character of one's natal land or surroundings; the precise referent is uncertain but contextually consistent with a list of geomantic arts. The three final ritual categories — pacifying, enriching, and fierce — are the standard three (sometimes four) tantric ritual activities and appear here in a pre-tantric Vinaya context simply as types of ritual manipulation, not technical tantric rites.  The passage on medical practices is a classical list of Āyurvedic and quasi-medical procedures. Several terms in the medical and ritual sections present interpretive challenges. The term rendered "excellent bulls" for ཁྱུ་མཆོག is literally "supreme of the herd" and almost certainly refers to a bull, though some traditions read it as referring to a fine horse or similar creature. The term མ་ཧེ (rendered "buffaloes") may refer to a specific breed or type of large bovine animal; this is the standard reading in comparative Pāli sources. The term རི་དགས་འཁྱིལ་པ and བྱ་རོག་འཁྱིལ་པ, rendered as divination by the circling of deer and crows respectively, follow the Pāli parallel closely. The term ཕོལ་མིག (rendered "eyes that are underdeveloped") is uncertain and may refer to cataracts, half-formed eyes, or similar ocular conditions in a medical-diagnostic context.  The phrase rendered "inner king" and "outer king" refers to the practice of predicting the outcomes of conflicts between a patron's own king and a rival or foreign king — a standard item in the canonical lists of wrong livelihood through political divination. The Tibetan nang gi rgyal po and phyi'i rgyal po carry exactly this sense.

The repeated astronomical list — solar and lunar deviations, conjunctions, meteors, horizon lights, and celestial drumming — appears to be a deliberate canonical enumeration and is rendered accordingly without condensation.  The sequence of similes here — the debtor, the sick man, the slave — belongs to the classical Nīvaraṇa-abandonment passage found in the Sāmaññaphala-sutta and parallel texts. The Tibetan at several points is formulaic and slightly elliptical; the translation follows the natural expansion the formula requires for coherent oral delivery. The term rendered "low-mindedness" throughout continues the rendering established in the preceding passage.  The five obstacles mentioned here are the five hindrances (nīvaraṇas): sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and regret, and doubt. The Tibetan does not enumerate them by name in this passage, so they are rendered collectively as "five obstacles" in accordance with the text.

The simile of the mountaintop lake is a classical canonical simile for the second dhyāna; it appears in the Pāli parallels (e.g., Sāmaññaphala Sutta, DN 2) and the correspondence is here well-preserved.  The passage moves through the third and fourth meditative concentrations (dhyānas) and then introduces the practice of creating a mind-made body, a topic that will continue in the following passage. The phrase rendered "complete purity and utter luminosity" translates a compound describing the quality of the fourth dhyāna; the Tibetan "kun du dag pa yongs su dkar ba" literally means "thoroughly pure and completely white," which in context denotes the mental radiance and purity characteristic of the fourth absorption. The simile of the gem at the end is left incomplete as the Tibetan passage breaks off mid-sentence; its continuation presumably follows in the next passage.  The phrase rendered "near afflictions" translates the Tibetan term for upakleśas, secondary or proximate afflictions, distinguished from the root afflictions. This is a standard Abhidharma technical usage and no emendation is required, though a general listener may understand it simply as "lesser defilements."

The simile of the snake and basket renders a term that could also be "snake-basket" or "wicker cage for snakes"; the exact implement is a container from which a snake is extracted, and "snake-basket" is the most natural rendering.  The passage contains two consecutive similes introducing the same superknowledge of the divine ear, which is not an error in translation but reflects the text's own repetitive structure. The second simile set appears to be a continuation or fuller version of the same teaching.

The term rendered "ivory-worker" translates a word that more literally means "bone-worker" or "craftsman working with a hard material such as tusk or bone." In context, the parallel with a potter suggests an artisan shaping a prepared material; ivory-worker is the standard interpretation.  The phrase rendered "intent on the Dharma in such a wrong spirit" translates "chos la yid dam bcas pa," which is somewhat elliptical. The most natural reading in this karmic context is that it refers to holding views or commitments toward the Dharma in the wrong way — possibly denying or misrepresenting it — consistent with the preceding description of calumny toward the noble ones and wrong view. This is a consequential interpretive choice worth flagging.

The term "proximate afflictions" renders "nye ba'i nyon mongs pa," referring to secondary or adjacent mental afflictions as distinct from the root afflictions, a standard Abhidharma category.  The phrase rendered "knowledge and conduct" translates the compound that corresponds to the Sanskrit vijjācaraṇasampanna, a standard epithet of the Buddha meaning "perfect in knowledge and conduct." The text is structured as a dialogue, apparently between the Buddha (speaking as Gautama) and a young brahmin, likely drawing on a sūtra parallel to the Tevijja-vacchagotta or a related discourse. The sequence of the four methods is introduced but the fourth portion is not yet complete in the passage given.  The list of brahmin seers follows the Tibetan transliteration closely. The Sanskrit names reconstructed are: Aṣṭaka, Vāmadeva, Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni (Tibetan: Ja ma dag ni), Aṅgiras, Bharadvāja, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Bhṛgu. The Tibetan rendering of some names is slightly irregular but the identifications are standard.

The image of the "four-doored house" built in the village is a recurring textual marker in this discourse for householder-style merit-making practice distinguished from forest or ascetic modes.

The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end, consistent with the supplied Tibetan which ends mid-description; the translation faithfully reproduces this open ending.  The name rendered "Padmaśīrṣa" (Tib. པདྨའི་སྙིང་པོ, literally "Essence/Heart of a Lotus") may alternatively be read as "Padmahṛdaya." The name rendered "Pokkharasādi" transliterates the Tibetan Pad+ma'i snying po, which is a Tibetan rendering of the Pāli Pokkharasādi, also known in Sanskrit as Puṣkarasārin or Puṣkarasādi. The name is kept consistent as Pokkharasādi throughout, as this is the established identification in scholarship, though the Tibetan literally means "Lotus Heart."

The phrase rendered "fallen into a lower state of existence" translates the Tibetan for a downfall or bad rebirth destiny, here in the context of Pokkharasādi's distress that his messenger behaved so poorly toward a genuinely great being.  The phrase rendered "drinking sesame oil" is literal; commentarial context suggests this old man was consuming sesame oil as part of some ritual or ascetic practice, and the brahmin's remark contrasts sincere Dharma-seekers with those pursuing worldly or ritualistic ends. The point of the anecdote is clear from context even without further gloss.

The name translated as "Māsuka" is rendered from the Tibetan "ma sdug" (literally "not agreeable" or "unpleasant"), which in this Pāli sūtra context corresponds to the brahmin student named Ambaṭṭha in the Pāli canon. The Tibetan translator appears to have rendered the name semantically rather than phonetically. This is a genuinely consequential philological point for identification of the text.  The repeated phrase rendered "continues as before, up to…" reflects a standard Indic and Tibetan abbreviated repetition formula in sūtra texts, signalling that the full wording of the enquiry after health is to be understood as repeated in each scenario.

The expression rendered "I am one who has risen / fully risen" translates the Tibetan "འཕགས་སོ / མངོན་པར་འཕགས་སོ," which in this context means the brahmin is affirming his attainment: he has risen, gone forth, or been elevated in a spiritual sense. The phrase rendered "Lotus-Heart" for Padmasnying is a translation of the Tibetan name pad+ma'i snying po; the text uses the Tibetan throughout and no Sanskrit equivalent is given, but the name corresponds to Sanskrit Padmasnying or Padmahṛdaya. The translation keeps it as "the brahmin Padmasnying" for consistency with the preceding passage.

The simile of the "hot seed" that is "rank and festering" and from which bees stay away is a somewhat cryptic condemnation of moral corruption: a foul seed attracts no beneficial contact. The triple characterization — hot, rank, festering — follows the Tibetan exactly.

The closing "The Blessed One reflected:" mirrors the Tibetan དབཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་དགོངས་པ at the end of the passage, indicating the passage breaks here and the Blessed One's subsequent reflection will follow in the next portion of the text.  The phrase rendered "a term of elevation" translates the Tibetan "tshig bla dags," which means a metaphorical or figurative expression, a term used in an elevated or indirect sense to denote something else. This is a standard Abhidharma-style explanatory formula.

The final sentence is left incomplete as the source passage itself ends mid-sentence, indicating a continuation follows.  The phrase rendered "wash your feet and lie down" is a conventional Indic hospitality formula; "earth" in the list alongside water and mustard oil likely refers to cleansing clay or ash used for foot-washing, a standard Vinaya-narrative detail.

The final paragraph repeats the ruling in slightly amplified form, which is typical of Vinaya canonical redaction. The phrase rendered "takes that as one's own affair" reflects a Vinaya idiom meaning treating the act as a personal matter, i.e., as something that does or should concern oneself.  The Tibetan "གནས་བརྟན་ཀུན་ཤེས་ཀཽཎྜི་ནྱས" identifies the elder as Kauṇḍinya with the epithet "Kun-shes" (he who knows all), the traditional Tibetan rendering of the Sanskrit name Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya (he who has come to know), the first disciple of the Buddha. The term rendered throughout as "the Vajjians" translates ཡུལ་སྤོང་བྱེད་པ (lit. "those who act as the Vajjians" or "the Vajji country-people"), which corresponds consistently to the Pāli Vajjī. The phrase rendered "kings among long-dwellers" translates a compound in which "gnas brtan rgyal po lta bu" means those who are like kings among the elders, i.e., the most senior and venerable monks. The phrase "born of joyful desire and arising moment by moment" renders a dense compound about craving for becoming; the Pali parallel (nandirāga) confirms this is craving accompanied by delight. The passage is mid-sentence at its conclusion, as the Tibetan continues directly into further conditions; it has been left open accordingly to signal continuation.  The phrase rendered "not troubling those who have come with concern for robes, alms-food" etc. reflects a reading in which arriving practitioners of the holy life are welcomed and not burdened with material anxiety. The Tibetan construction here is slightly compressed, but the sense is clear from parallel Pāli versions of this discourse, where the monks are praised for ensuring visiting brethren are well provided for rather than left to worry over requisites.

The list item translated as "gossip" renders a Tibetan term literally meaning "speech about towns and villages," a standard idiom in the Vinaya literature for worldly gossip and frivolous talk about mundane affairs.  The seven limbs of awakening passage presents a compressed syntactic structure in which each limb is implicitly qualified by the same four characteristics — abiding in seclusion, dispassion, cessation, and transformation through relinquishment — that are explicitly stated for mindfulness and equanimity. The village name rendered in Tibetan as "Nāḍa" (དམར་བུ་ཅན) is literally "the reddish one" in Tibetan. The phrase rendered "fetters that are not in conformity with the higher part" translates the Tibetan for the Pali/Sanskrit distinction between the five lower fetters (orambhāgīya saṃyojana) and the five higher fetters (uddhambhāgīya saṃyojana). Those who abandon the five higher fetters are non-returners (anāgāmin), reborn in pure-abode realms and attaining nirvāṇa there without returning to the desire realm; those who abandon only the three fetters and thin out desire are once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin); those who abandon the three fetters entirely and enter the stream are stream-enterers (srotāpanna). The Tibetan here presents these soteriological categories by description rather than by the standard Sanskrit technical names, and the translation follows the Tibetan phrasing while preserving the doctrinal referents.

The name "Rabhassona" in the preceding passage corresponds here in the Tibetan to "Rab brtson," which literally means "Diligent" or "Supremely Striving." The passage on the "Dharma Mirror" presents a notable doctrinal framing: the four factors of confirmed faith in the Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha, and noble discipline serve here as a kind of interior "mirror" by which a noble disciple can verify their own attainment of stream-entry. This is consistent with the standard Pāli parallel in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, where the same teaching is called the Dhammādāsa. The Tibetan term here rendered "category" is rnam grangs, which strictly means "synonym" or "enumeration," but in this stock phrase it functions as a name-category or class-designation for the teaching.  The four-fold formula of diligence rendered here corresponds to the classical teaching on the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), presented here in an expanded, repetitive sūtra style. The fourfold application of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) is similarly given in the abbreviated form standard in Pāli and Sanskrit sūtra parallels. The phrase rendered "grasps the mind and applies it" translates a stock formula for mental effort and sustained engagement. The "signless meditative absorption" is the formless samādhi in which no characteristic marks are taken as object. The phrase rendered "reinforces the life-sustaining formations and relinquishes the will-to-live" translates a technically precise Pāli/Sanskrit concept: the Tathāgata, through meditative power, deliberately suspends the life-force (āyusaṃskāra) rather than allowing it to continue naturally. The term rendered as "Mātṛkā" in the third scenario refers to the Abhidharma matrix-texts or numerical summary lists — sometimes rendered "doctrinal summaries" — and is paired here with sūtra-holders and Vinaya-holders as the third category of specialist monk. The term rendered "monks who uphold the Mātṛkā" translates a phrase that in Tibetan reads literally "those who uphold the mother-like" or "those who uphold the matrix text." Mātṛkā here refers to the Abhidharma or proto-Abhidharma summaries, the numerical and categorical lists that formed the basis of doctrinal analysis, a standard third category alongside sūtra and Vinaya in early canonical classification. The fourfold structure here is the teaching of the "four great references" or "four great proclamations" (mahāpadesa in Pali), which authenticates teachings by checking them against sūtra, Vinaya, and the nature of reality. The gesture of placing the robe over one shoulder before addressing the Buddha is a standard Vinaya posture of respectful supplication and is rendered accordingly.  The summary verse near the middle of the passage is a colophon-style mnemonic listing the topics of the fifty-second section. The names "Cāpāla" and "Rurutā" are rendered from the Tibetan phonetics; the Sanskrit forms may vary by recension. The river name "Kakuṭṭhā" is the standard Pāli form; the Tibetan reads "Kakusta," which corresponds to it. The phrase rendered "Great Elephant" likely refers to the Blessed One himself, as "great elephant" (mahānāga) is a standard epithet of the Buddha in Vinaya literature.  The name "Silāyin" renders the Tibetan sgyu rtsal shes kyi bu ring du 'phur, which is a somewhat unusual construction. The Tibetan appears to preserve the name of a wandering ascetic teacher known in Pāli sources as Pukkusa Mallaputta's teacher, Āḷāra Kālāma in some parallels, but the specific name here — "Silāyin the Magician" — translates sgyu rtsal shes as "one who knows magical arts" and bu ring du 'phur as "son who travels far through the air." It is possible the full phrase is an epithet or title rather than a personal name with patronymic; the rendering here treats it as a name-cum-epithet consistent with the narrative context. The parallel Pāli passage in the Mahāparinibbānasutta (DN 16) names this figure as Pukkusa Mallaputta, a disciple of Āḷāra Kālāma, which confirms the general identification but does not resolve the specific Tibetan nomenclature with certainty.  The town name rendered throughout as "Ātumā" corresponds to the Pāli Āṭumā, a known location in canonical texts. The Tibetan spelling ཨ་དུ་མ་ཡ and ཨ་དུ་མན་དུར reflects this place name with case suffixes.

The proper name "Gyad" renders a Tibetan transcription of what in Pāli sources is the Oḍḍhaddha or similar clan affiliation; the exact Sanskrit or Pāli identification of this clan name in the Tibetan transmission is uncertain and may warrant further comparison with parallel Pāli versions of this sūtra episode, which appears to correspond to the Aṭṭhaka-sutta or a related account of the storm at Āṭumā.  The river name rendered as "Kakudhā" is the standard Sanskrit equivalent of the Tibetan "dbyig ldan" — this is the river near Kuśinagara where, according to the Mahāparinirvāṇa accounts, the Buddha bathed before his final passing.

The phrase translated as "equal and unequalled" renders Tibetan "mnyam pa dang mi mnyam pa," a classical paradoxical formulation meaning that these two meal offerings are equal to each other and yet unequalled by any other — a standard doctrinal expression found in Pali and Sanskrit parinirvāṇa literature (Pali: "samasama").  The monk named "Sunakkhatta" appears here as "འདུན་པ" in the Tibetan. This is a Pali name rendered into Tibetan; the form given here follows the name as it appears in the context. The identification is reasonably secure from parallel passages in the Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra tradition.

The "brahmic penalty" (tshangs pa'i chad pa) refers to a specific formal disciplinary measure in the Vinaya tradition: the community collectively ceases to speak with the offending monk, effectively cutting off all normal interaction. It is the inverse of a proclamation and is called "brahmic" because Brahmā himself is said to observe this form of silent withdrawal.

The final verse ends mid-sentence in the source passage as given; the translation preserves this incompleteness, as the text breaks off at that point.  The phrase rendered "those who hold the Abhidharma" translates a term literally meaning "those who hold the Mātṛkā," an early term for the Abhidharma matrix texts; this is a standard identification in the tradition and requires no further gloss.

The "ten powers of wisdom" refers to the ten powers (daśabala) of a Tathāgata, here specifically characterized in terms of wisdom. The verse line identifies the monk who taught as one whom the Buddha himself had declared to be foremost in wisdom, a reference consistent with the figure of Śāriputra in comparable narrative contexts, though the text does not name him explicitly here.  The phrase rendered "this great feast of Dharma, this singular thing" translates a construction in which "great feast of Dharma" and "singular" describe the Buddha's unsurpassed Dharma teaching as a unique and peerless treasure now lost to the world. The Tibetan "ཆོས་ཀྱི་ལོངས་སྤྱོད་ཆེན་པོ་འབའ་ཞིག་པོ" could also be rendered "this one sole great enjoyment of Dharma," with "sole" or "singular" emphasizing its irreplaceability; the rendering above preserves that sense.  The passage's rhetorical structure is slightly irregular in the Tibetan, repeating the formula about the wheel-turning king's retinue partway through the Ānanda parallel before the second set of four qualities. This appears to be a textual feature of the Tibetan rather than a translational issue, and the translation follows it faithfully.

"Sāketa" renders གནས་བཅས, which is a standard Tibetan equivalent for that city. "Campā" renders ཙམ་པ.

The term རྩང (staircase or landing of a gate) is rendered as "staircase" in context with gate architecture, though "pillar" or "post" is occasionally proposed; "staircase" is the more standard reading here and fits the architectural list.  The passage lists several Sanskrit flower names transliterated into Tibetan. Where standard Sanskrit equivalents are well-attested — utpala (blue lotus), padma (lotus), kumuda (white water lily), puṇḍarīka-class whites, campaka, mālikā, navamālikā, yūthikā — they have been rendered accordingly. The term rendered "yellow jasmine" for skya snar is an approximation; the Sanskrit equivalent may be tagara or a related aromatic. Dhānuskari is a phonetic transliteration whose botanical identification is uncertain.

The phrase "King Mahāsudarśana" appears here for the first time by name in this passage — in the Tibetan it reads rgyal po legs mthong chen po, literally "the great king of excellent appearance," the standard Tibetan rendering of Mahāsudarśana. This name was used in the preceding portion already, so it has been rendered consistently.

The section ends mid-sentence in the source text; the translation breaks at exactly the same point.  The term rendered "lord" in the people's address to the charioteer is literally "the god" (lha), used here as a royal honorific for the king — a common usage in Tibetan sūtra literature for a cakravartin monarch, not a reference to a divine being. This honorific flavor is preserved contextually without cluttering the prose.

The twelve sounds: the text explicitly numbers them as twelve (sounded in the prior passage and the count closed here). The list in the preceding passage contains ten items; this passage adds the paṭaha drum, music, song, and flute (four more), but also includes three proclamatory sounds ("Generosity has been given," "Merit has been made," "Those who fast have taken up ethical conduct"), bringing the total to twelve as stated. The grouping is internally consistent in the Tibetan.  The phrase rendered "Dharma-fitting palace" translates a compound meaning a palace built in accordance with the Dharma, that is, through righteous means. The repetition of the offering and refusal cycle two and three times is a standard formulaic trope in this literature indicating persistent, earnest entreaty. The honorific verbal forms directed at the king have been rendered with appropriate dignity without being archaic.  The passage includes a standard fascicle-division colophon marking the boundary between the fifty-third and fifty-fourth fascicles of the Vinaya Kṣudrakavastu; it has been rendered in plain prose as it appears in the text.

The architectural terminology presents consistent interpretive challenges. Terms such as ཀ་རྟེན, ཀ་ཞུ, བྲེ་ཕུལ, གདུང་, གདུང་ཕྲན, མདུན་གདུང, གདུང་པོ་ཆེ, བ་གམ, སྤང་ལེབ, ལན་ཀན, གཟུངས་གཟེར, རྟེན་མ, and གདུང་བུ refer to specific structural elements of a multi-story palace. The renderings given — base-support, column-cap, bracket-block, crossbeam, secondary rafter, front beam, main roof beam, wall-panel, wall-slab, railing, dowel-pin, support-post, baluster-shaft — reflect reasonable correspondences to traditional South Asian timber architecture but cannot be verified with certainty against the original Sanskrit architectural vocabulary.  The throne furnishings — Golika cloth, Mentri cushions, Armonig cushions, Kāliṅga cloth — are Sanskrit loanwords transcribed into Tibetan (go li ka, men tri, ar mo nig, kā liṅ ka) referring to specific luxury textiles and furnishing styles known in the Indian courtly tradition; their precise identification is uncertain, and they are rendered here by approximate transliteration following scholarly convention.

The term rendered "owl-feather cushions" (za 'ug gi stan) literally means a cushion made of or styled after the owl; this may refer to a particular style of soft cushioning rather than literal feathers, but the exact referent is uncertain.  The phrase rendered "five-part instrument" translates a term referring to a musical instrument with five components or registers — likely the classical Indian vīṇā or similar; the exact instrument is not specified in the text. The phrase "fine woven cloth garments" renders a term for a type of high-quality textile; the precise identification is uncertain but the rendering conveys the general sense adequately. The "royal sage's holy celibate life" renders a compound meaning the brahmacarya practiced by a royal ṛṣi — a life of celibacy and renunciation while remaining nominally a king, a recognized category in Indian Buddhist narrative literature.  The elephant king's name, rendered here as "Nearby Restoration," translates the Tibetan ཉེ་བའི་གསོ་སྦྱོང་, literally "the nearby poṣadha," where གསོ་སྦྱོང་ (poṣadha) can refer to the Buddhist observance day but in this cosmological context is a proper epithet of the elephant king. The rendering follows the literal meaning and may correspond to a Sanskrit epithet such as Upapoṣadha; this is a well-known name in wheel-turning monarch narratives. The chariot name དགའ་དབྱངས་ (Joyful Sound) and the horse king སྤྲིན་གྱི་ཤུགས་ཅན་ (Cloud-Force) are straightforward literal renderings of Tibetan epithets.  The term rendered "Near-Observance" for the elephant king's name (Tibetan: ཉེ་བའི་གསོ་སྦྱོང) literally means "near poṣadha" or "approaching the observance day." It is a proper name in this narrative context and the rendering attempts to convey its literal sense. The exact Sanskrit original is uncertain; some versions read differently.

The phrase rendered "Three-Balconied" for the mansion name (ཁང་པ་རྩེག་མ་བ་གམ་ཅན) literally means "the multi-storied mansion possessing three balconies/terraces," treated here as a proper epithet of that category's lead example.  The phrase rendered "frontier lords" translates a compound meaning lords of the border regions or districts, here prefaced by "jewel minister" as the lead exemplar; this matches the preceding passage's usage. The repetition of the full list of possessions in both the queen's speech and the retinue's reply is faithful to the Tibetan, which genuinely repeats the catalogue twice. The phrase "ཁམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཕྲན་" in the queen's initial speech and "མཐའི་རྒྱལ་ཕྲན་" in the retinue's reply differ slightly in wording but appear to refer to the same category; "frontier lords" is used for both.  The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end, describing distances from Kuśāvatī. This is simply where the supplied passage ends and is not a translation problem.

The phrase rendered "reborn on an equal footing" translates a term meaning "born equally" or "born in parity" in the Brahmā world, indicating rebirth at the same level as the Brahmā gods — a standard doctrinal point about the fruit of the four divine abodes.  The epithet "the capable" (Tib. thub pa) applied to the gods of many hundreds of kalpas is unusual. It likely refers to gods who have accumulated the power (thub pa = capable/enduring) over vast cosmic time, but it may be a compressed reference to gods associated with a particular class of long-lived beings. The rendering reflects the literal Tibetan without over-interpreting.

The phrase rendered "radiant proximity" translates 'od pa bzhin nye bar gnas pa, literally "dwelling near, like light" — a slightly opaque phrase likely referring to the supernatural quality of being luminously present and accessible. This is a genuinely uncertain reading.  The passage moves between two distinct narrative threads: first, a past-life story set during the time of buddha Kāśyapa, in which the duty-monk's aspiration leads to his eventual rebirth as an arhat under Śākyamuni; and second, the Blessed One's instructions to Ānanda on relic veneration after his passing. The shift is abrupt in the Tibetan and has been rendered accordingly.

The phrase rendered "duty-monk" translates dge skos, the monk assigned rotating administrative duties in a monastery; this technical Vinaya term has been rendered descriptively for clarity in speech.

The aspiration prayer is syntactically complex in the Tibetan and involves an embedded prophecy (lung bstan) within the aspirational frame; the rendering preserves this structure as faithfully as readability permits.  The phrase rendered "warrior-nobles" translates a term referring to the Malla clan, the ruling warrior aristocracy of Kuśinagara (Sanskrit: Malla), who in Pāli sources are consistently called Mallā. The Tibetan renders this as "gyad," a term for powerful warriors or heroes. Keeping "warrior-nobles" maintains the social register without importing the Sanskrit clan name mid-sentence, which would interrupt the flow.

The phrase "foundations of training" renders the standard formula for lay refuge and the five precepts. The Tibetan here gives only the refuge formula explicitly; the precepts are implied by "foundations of training."

The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end, as the passage supplied ends there; no content has been added or invented beyond what the Tibetan provides.  The name rendered "Rabjā" is Tibetan for "Pramudita," meaning "Greatly Joyful," and functions as a proper name for the gandharva king. The epithet Kauśika is a standard name for Śakra (Indra). The five kinds of seeing refers to the five considerations by which a bodhisattva in Tuṣita surveys before taking his final birth: the right time, the right continent, the right land, the right clan, and the right mother. The "thirty-six billion" renders bye ba phrag sum bcu rtsa drug, literally thirty-six sets of ten thousand, i.e., 360,000,000; some editions may vary in this figure.  The epithet "gandharva and more" renders ང་དྲི་ཟ་ཏེ་པོར་ཡིན་ནོ, where ཏེ་པོ conveys "and something beyond" or "and more besides" — a pointed double meaning, since the Blessed One is both literally playing the role of a gandharva musician and is, of course, far more than that. This wordplay is integral to the narrative's irony and is preserved in the rendering.  The phrase rendered "the last couch" for ཐ་མའི་གཟིམས་མལ is a reference to the Blessed One's final resting place before parinirvāṇa, a standard Pali and Sanskrit idiom. The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end, which reflects the source text's continuation into the next segment.  The phrase rendered as "blazed with a brilliant, clear radiance" translates the Tibetan idiom me lhan ne lhang nger gyur, a vivid sensory expression suggesting the grove lit up or shone brightly; the exact nuance is picturesque rather than technically doctrinal.

The city rendered "Kuśinagara" appears in the Tibetan as grong khyer rtsa can, literally "the city with grass," which is a Tibetan calque for Kuśinagara (Pāli: Kusinārā); context and tradition confirm the identification.  The six teachers named are the well-known "six heterodox teachers" of the Pāli tradition. The Tibetan names correspond to Pūraṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta (the Jain leader Mahāvīra), and Ajita Kesakambalī or Kaccāyana. The rendering follows standard identifications from parallel Pāli sources (Dīgha Nikāya, Mahāparinibbānasutta). The verse section is syntactically compressed in the Tibetan and the passage ends mid-sentence in the source, which is reflected faithfully by ending the translation at the same point.  The passage contains Subhadra's parinirvāṇa blessing-visions, which are part of a canonical narrative preserved in several Vinaya and sūtra traditions. The "five places" Subhadra intends to bless are enumerated in what follows; only the first part of the list appears in the passage translated here, so the full sequence is not yet visible.

The exchange between Subhadra and the Blessed One — "do you speak in order for yourself to pass into nirvāṇa, or for the Blessed One to pass into nirvāṇa?" — reflects a delicate grammatical ambiguity in classical Tibetan that the dialogue format itself resolves: Subhadra clarifies that he is requesting the Blessed One's consent to his own prior nirvāṇa, not commenting on the Buddha's.  The name "Rabzang" renders the Tibetan kun du rgyu rab bzang, which is a Tibetan translation of what is likely a Sanskrit name meaning something like "excellent wanderer" or "supremely good peripatetic." In the preceding passage it was rendered "Rabzang" for consistency; the full meaning is "the Excellent Wanderer." This is the figure known in Pali sources as Subhadda, the last direct disciple of the historical Buddha — though the narrative here differs from the Pali account in significant ways.

The phrase "joints severed and articulations splitting" renders gnad rnams ni chad, tshigs rnams ni 'bye ba, a description of the severe physical pain the dying Buddha was experiencing, understood in the tradition as signaling the approach of parinirvāṇa.  The epithet "the city of Kuśa" renders གྲོང་ཁྱེར་རྩྭ་ཅན, literally "the city of grass," which most probably corresponds to Kuśinagara (Kuśa being the sacred grass); the earlier passage rendered it as "Kusināra," so consistency is maintained by the phrase "city of Kuśa." The phrase སྲོག་སྡུག་པའི་སྐྱབས, "refuge precious as life itself," is a somewhat unusual compound meaning shelter that is as dear to them as their own lives, or alternatively that he offered refuge at the cost of his own life; both meanings are in play and the translation preserves the resonance without choosing artificially between them.  The horse's name, literally "Knows-the-Art-of-War" or "Knows-Military-Craft," is rendered "Wise-Knowing" throughout for consistency with the established translation. The precise nuance of the Tibetan compound (རྟ་ཅང་ཤེས, "horse knowing the art") is one of military skill rather than generic wisdom, but "Wise-Knowing" is preserved here as the established proper name rendering. A note on the pool's bird species: kāraṇḍava is a standard Sanskrit waterfowl name retained in the text; ངུར་པ (heron) follows the most common identification. The bird ཤང་ཤང་ཏེའུ is an uncertain compound; it may refer to a type of flycatcher or similar bird and is rendered generically.  The verse near the end is the well-known karma-stanza found across several Vinaya and Abhidharma contexts; it is rendered here according to its standard doctrinal meaning. The phrase rendered "waiting like a flame near at hand" translates a metaphor implying that the karma is present and luminous, poised for inevitable fruition — a standard image for karma that is "definite to be experienced" in this very life or in a near future life. The term rendered "long-lived Supriya" (Tibetan: tshe dang ldan pa Rab bzang) is a standard honorific form of address for an elder monk; "long-lived" renders the formulaic tshe dang ldan pa (Sanskrit āyuṣman). "Cañjaśa" is kept consistent with the preceding passage's rendering of the horse's name.  The epithet "Anāthapiṇḍada" rendered here as "Sorrowless" follows the Tibetan mya ngan med, which means "without sorrow." This is distinct from the famous lay patron Anāthapiṇḍada of the Pāli and Sanskrit traditions; in the Tibetan, the name given is mya ngan med, meaning "sorrowless" or "Anātha" in the sense of being free from grief. The rendering follows the Tibetan literally throughout.

The phrase rendered "knower of the world" translates 'jig rten mkhyen pa, a standard epithet of the Buddha corresponding to Sanskrit lokavid.

The syntax of the god's aspiration prayer at the close is somewhat compressed in the Tibetan; the translation unpacks it to make the sequence of intended events clear for the listener.  The phrase "matted fiery hair" renders the Tibetan me ba ral pa can literally. This is most likely a reference to the Jaṭilas, the fire-worshipping ascetics with matted hair, such as the Kāśyapa brothers and their followers, who were among the earliest converts. The Vinaya tradition preserves a specific exemption for this group from the four-month probationary period required of other non-Buddhist wanderers. The identity of "Subhadrā" as the god named Supriya or Subhadra, the brahmin boy disciple of Kāśyapa referenced in the preceding passage, is consistent with the narrative logic of the prophecy section immediately prior.  The twelve-fold wheel of Dharma refers to the standard formulation of the Four Noble Truths each presented in three aspects of recognition, application, and attainment, yielding twelve aspects in total.

The list of twelve textual categories corresponds to the traditional twelvefold classification of canonical literature known in Sanskrit as the dvādaśāṅga-pravacana. The rendering of individual categories follows their standard Tibetan-Sanskrit correspondences: sūtra, geya (mixed prose and verse), vyākaraṇa (prophetic declaration), gāthā (verse), udāna (intentional saying), nidāna (origin narrative), avadāna (story of spiritual attainment), itivṛttaka (account of past deeds), jātaka (birth story), vaipulya (extensive teaching), adbhutadharma (marvellous Dharma), and upadeśa (established doctrine).

The phrase rendered "nets" in the list of monastic requisites is genuinely uncertain; this term may refer to a kind of filtering cloth or strainer used by monks, and its precise identification is debated among commentators.  The phrase rendered "some shall go with a remainder of the aggregates still present" refers to rebirth in a higher realm rather than nirvāṇa — that is, they attain a fortunate rebirth but not yet final liberation. This reflects the classical distinction between those who attain liberation at death versus those reborn in higher realms due to faith. The repetition of the four sacred sites formula in this passage is faithful to the source, which genuinely repeats the full formula multiple times in succession. The phrase "prophesy the answer" renders lung bstan pa, which in this conversational context means "to give an authoritative declaration or answer," not eschatological prophecy in a narrow sense — though the same term covers both meanings elsewhere.  The phrase rendered "the eye of peaceful, unmoving stillness" translates a description of the physical eyes of the deceased body — the Blessed One's eyes remain open and still, serene and motionless. This is a recognized Indian literary and doctrinal topos for the moment of parinirvāṇa; the Tibetan zhiba mi g.yo ba'i spyan refers literally to eyes that are peaceful and unmoving, a sign the body has entered final cessation.

The sequence of absorptions described here — ascending through the four dhyānas and four formless spheres to the cessation of perception and feeling, then descending in reverse, and finally ascending again to the fourth dhyāna where parinirvāṇa occurs — is the canonical account found across multiple recensions of the Mahāparinirvāṇa literature and is doctrinally significant: the Buddha's final passing occurs from the fourth dhyāna, not from the cessation attainment.  The phrase "body-servant" for ལུས་འཕགས་མའི་བུ" is textually odd and may reflect a title or epithet of Ajātaśatru that is obscure; the Tibetan literally reads "son of the one whose body is noble" or possibly "son of Vaidehī" (a known epithet of Ajātaśatru's mother Queen Vaidehī). The rendering here follows context and parallel passages in this genre. Some translators render this as "son of Vaidehī," which is doctrinally standard in accounts of Ajātaśatru.

The term "rootless faith" (རྩ་བ་མེད་པའི་དད་པ) is a technical term from Vinaya and narrative literature describing Ajātaśatru's particular form of devotion, rooted in remorse for parricide rather than in prior spiritual accumulation — it is left as a doctrinal term of art here.

The gosirṣa sandalwood treatment across seven bowls of butter is a resuscitation procedure attested in other versions of the Mahāparinirvāṇa narrative cycle.  The phrase rendered "gods of the Mighty One" translates a compound that literally reads "the gods, as many as exist, of the Capable One / the Mighty One" — a standard epithet for the Buddha as "the Sage" or "Capable One." The syntax here is compressed and the sentence structure slightly irregular; the taunt that follows is attributed to those gods, directed at the lamenting monks.

The stupa described as "crowned with a warrior's diadem" renders a compound suggesting a commemorative or reliquary monument ornamented in the manner of a warrior's crown — the precise referent is a specific stupa in the Kuśinagara region, named by the manner of its construction or ornamentation.

The passage ends mid-sentence, consistent with the provided text being a fragment; no translation is invented beyond what is given.  The phrase rendered "those who lived on wages" translates a term for those maintained by milk-whey or similar provisions, indicating a class of dependents or hired servants in the household; the exact social category is context-dependent but the general sense of household dependents is clear. The phrase "into the realm of complete cessation without remainder" renders the standard technical compound for the nirvāṇa without residue, literally the "nirvāṇa-realm without remaining aggregates," which is the parinirvāṇa. The final phrase "venerating and adorning him" renders a sequence of three terms of veneration that slightly overlap; the translation condenses them naturally for oral delivery.  The phrase rendered "golden bier" translates a term meaning golden stretcher or carrying frame, used to bear the body in procession; "bier" is the most natural English equivalent in a funerary context. The phrase rendered "shrine adorned with a diadem by the Mallas" translates a Tibetan expression referring to a stūpa (caitya) crowned or decorated with a diadem-like finial by the Mallas. The Pāli parallel (Mahāparinibbānasutta, DN 16) identifies this as the Makuṭabandhana shrine of the Mallas, and "diadem-bound" is its standard epithet. This is preserved in the translation as "shrine adorned with a diadem by the Mallas" to reflect both the Tibetan wording and the known referent.  The "champion" who raised the garland on the stūpa is the same figure referenced in the preceding passage as a hero or strong-man among the Mallas; the term rendered "champion" translates the Tibetan word for a warrior of exceptional strength.

The elder who speaks the improper words is understood by the tradition to be Subhadra the Elder, distinct from Subhadra the last personal disciple of the Buddha; the passage becomes the canonical occasion that motivates Mahākāśyapa to convene the First Council. This is doctrinally significant context, though the name does not appear in the passage itself.  The epithet ཚེ་དང་ལྡན་པ་སྐུལ་བྱེད་ཆེན་པོ rendered as "Mahāmaudgalyāyana" follows the standard identification in this narrative context, though the Tibetan literally means "the great impeller" or "the great instigator," which corresponds to Maudgalyāyana's epithet in some traditions.
